speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING MAXIMUM INCOME LEVEL AND MERCHANT BUILDERS' LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement on government housing policy. As I have repeatedly said in this house, housing is a subject under continuing review by the government under flexible policies we have introduced to meet changing conditions, for conditions do change sometimes overnight in this industry, an industry that plays such a significant role in the nation's economy.
Because of geographical and climatic conditions we all know that the winter months in many parts of Canada are traditionally difficult ones on the employment market, particularly where construction workers are concerned. Furthermore, there is in Canada today a demand for new housing by home owner applicants that cannot be satisfied by the present income requirements of $5,000 to $5,600 relating to government mortgage loans.
It is therefore the government's intention to try to meet this demand by easing existing limitations, and at the same time to provide greater work opportunities during the coming winter months. The present direct lending policy was restricted for fiscal reasons. We are now prepared to relax these restrictions to provide greater employment. To attain this dual objective we recognize that the resources of the efficient and highly organized house building industry in this country must be employed to the fullest and best advantage. At the same time measures to produce more new housing must not be permitted to add to the present stock of unsold dwellings.
With these considerations in mind, two steps are to be taken. First, effective September 1 the income limitation on applicants seeking direct loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be increased to $7,000 with $200 in upward adjustments for larger families to a maximum of $7,600. Second, also effective on September 1 the corporation will receive applications for direct loans from merchant builders as distinguished from speculative builders, provided the house on which the loan is to be made has been
presold to a bona fide purchaser whose income does not exceed $7,000 or up to $7,600 in the case of larger families.
In both instances applications will be received immediately for processing but loan commitments, of course, will not be issued until September 1. After November 30 we will revert to loans to home owner applicants only on terms and conditions to be announced at that time. In the case of builders, an advance on the mortgage loan will not be made until title has been transferred to the purchaser and evidence of the assumption of mortgage provided. Furthermore, a builder-sponsored application will not be accepted if the builder already has a stock of unsold houses or insists upon reproducing a house type of which there is already a number completed and unsold in the immediate market area.
Hon. members will no doubt wish to ask me what effect this change in policy will have on the over-all housing program and what number of starts may be achieved this year. First of all let me say that the new arrangement is not designed to produce any particular number of new starts this fall. It is tailored rather to activate verifiable demand or to meet the demand for new loans within the designated income limits and to permit builders to seek out this demand. It is difficult to forecast what added volume of C.M.H.C. lending will result from this change, and I am not going to attempt to do so. Last winter, however, in the house, as hon. members will recall, I estimated that new housing starts in 1960 would probably reach 120,000 to 125,000 units. The effect of this special arrangement which I have just announced for the next three months will likely result in total housing starts somewhat higher than this.
I have taken this opportunity to make an early announcement of the new requirements to give merchant builders ample time in which to make their plans. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the plan I have outlined accomplishes several things which I should like to mention. First, it assists those Canadian families-well, they are already pouring cold water on the enterprise. I might expect this from the opposition but from my dear friend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) it is more than I can understand. He is inuring me to the future. I hope this will be the end of any cold water.

Housing
As I say, the plan assists those Canadian families who still have an urgent need for homes of their own; second, it utilizes to advantage the facilities of the house building industry. Don't bother with that water; I am used to paddling my own canoe.

Mr. Speaker, on July 8 the Soviet embassy in Ottawa informed the Department of External Affairs that they had received a telegram from the captain of the Soviet scientific ship, the Lomonosov, reporting that an unidentified airplane had flown over the ship at a low altitude. The captain recommended that these flights should cease in order to avoid accidents.
On receiving this information the Department of External Affairs approached the Department of National Defence and instructions were issued that Canadian aircraft should not fly at low altitudes over the Lomonosov, which had been known to be operating off the Canadian coast outside of territorial waters. The Soviet embassy was informed on July 8 of the action which had been taken.
On July 14 the Canadian ambassador in Moscow was called to the Soviet foreign office to receive a copy of a complaint which the Soviet government had made to the United

speechtext:
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier-Lasalle asked a question concerning the noise caused by jet aircraft at Dorval airport. As a result of study by departmental operational officials and consultation with the air fines, a series of operational rules have been put into effect which should improve the situation. Radar traffic control is to give departing aircraft courses to steer to avoid built-up areas wherever possible, and mandatory use of preferential runways for both takeoffs and landings to avoid built-up areas whenever weather conditions permit will become effective immediately. The air fines are adopting the climb take-off and power setting procedures approved for jet aircraft by the international air transport association, while on instrument approaches the I.L.S. glide path will be intercepted at 1,500 feet rather than 1,000 feet to eliminate procedural turns at lower altitudes and allow more time for power settings for descent.
No training take-offs and landings are being allowed during the night hours, and no scheduled take-offs and landings are in the timetable after midnight. This situation is to be continued. The air lines have also been informed that the record with regard to delayed take-offs after midnight must be so materially improved as to eliminate this difficulty, and have given their assurance that this will be the case. My officials are maintaining a close and continuing review of the situation.

the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. C-68, to amend the Income Tax Act.
He said: Hon. members are aware that with respect to Bill No. C-68, to amend the Income Tax Act the Senate has made two amendments. They were reported to the house on Thursday, July 14, and printed in the Votes and Proceedings of this house on that day at page 773.
These are not far-reaching amendments, Mr. Speaker. In each case they strike from the bill a subclause. There is no constitutional question at issue here because in moving to strike these out the Senate acted at the request of the Minister of Finance.
The two clauses, Mr. Speaker, are not ones that enter into questions pertaining to the balance of ways and means; they are of a technical and legislative nature. The first relates to clause 18 of the bill respecting the provision for recapture of the capital cost allowances on depreciable property distributed by a trust or estate to a beneficiary. In the other clause, which is No. 24, the amendment provided thereby to section 83 A of the act contemplated the insertion of the word "exclusively" in two places. This amendment, it was indicated to the house, was for the purpose of giving legislative confirmation to the administrative practice of the Department of National Revenue. The department is quite satisfied that this practice can stand in the courts without the necessity for any legislative confirmation.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am moving concurrence in the two amendments.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the minister satisfied himself that his action is not in conflict with standing order 63. I have had some misgivings on it, but if he is satisfied-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. These amendments were made by the Senate committee at the request of the Minister of Finance, in this respect following the practice that has existed for some years. The point that you have raised concerning the rule of this house has no application to this situation.

While these amendments are technical they are not unimportant, Mr. Speaker. Since a thorough discussion took place in the Senate, both in the banking and commerce committee of that place and on second

reading of the bill in the Senate, I do not propose to deal with the issues involved. The printed report of the proceedings of the final sittings of the Senate committee on banking and commerce unfortunately is not available yet from the printer, but the chairman of that committee gave a very full explanation of what had taken place with relation to these amendments when he spoke in the Senate on July 13. For those outside the house who are interested in these amendments, and there will be a number, I commend the reports of the proceedings of the Senate banking and commerce committee dated June 30 and July 6, and the third one which has not yet been printed.
In addition to making the amendments before us, the distinguished lawyers and others who composed the Senate banking and commerce committee also made a very close examination of section 33. They considered making amendments, but after further discussion with the officers of the Department of Finance decided not to do so.
We had a rather interesting explanation from the Minister of Finance that we have no constitutional issue here because these amendments were made at his request. That may be, Mr. Speaker, but I point out that the section was very carefully criticized by the eminent lawyers and others on the Senate banking and commerce committee, as evidenced by the reports of the committee proceedings. The members of the Senate suggested to the officers of the department that their criticisms were worth while, and they asked the officers to go back to the Minister of Finance with an indication that they proposed to make amendments and ask for further consideration by the minister. The minister has, of course, announced that he has withdrawn two of the items originally in the draft bill.
While we are discussing Bill No. C-68, I wonder whether the minister's attention has been drawn to the article with respect to taxes in the last issue of the Financial Post written by Mr. John C. McDonald, a well known expert in the tax field. He deals particularly with the amendments in the bill relating to the new sections 136 (12a) and (12b). He reports something that, in view of our amendments to the section, I think should have the immediate attention of the minister.
The article is headlined, "Department Traps Unwary in Mailing Date Mix-up". Although we have declared in the bill that the effective date upon which appeals from assessments will be based will be the actual mailing date, the article suggests that it has become the practice of the department

to put a date on the assessment notice that is frequently several days later than the date when the assessment notice is actually put in the mail. As Mr. McDonald points out in the article, this means that if your notice is dated April 25 but is mailed to you on May 1 the department may have your appeal thrown out because you have not filed your objection within the allowable 90 days. The unwary person may not retain the envelope with the postmark on it and may find that he has lost several days as a result of this rather peculiar and, I would suggest, perhaps shabby practice on the part of the taxing authorities.
In view of the amendment the minister has advanced making it very clear that the effective date is the actual date of mailing, I wonder whether the Minister of Finance will not consult with his colleague the Minister of National Revenue, to see whether this is indeed a trap that is not desirable and whether the practice could not be altered.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was going to ask for a copy of the bill, which I understood was amended in the committee. Would the minister be good enough to give a short summary of what happened in the committee and tell us which of the representations were met, which were not, and for what reasons?

Mr. Chairman, I had rather assumed that the hon. member and other members interested in the bill would have read the report of the committee that met to deal with the matter.
There were two amendments suggested to clause 2 and when we reach that clause I shall ask one of my colleagues to move those amendments. The other matters discussed in the committee, which met I believe for some four hours, would require quite a bit of reading on my part if I were to elucidate them. I assumed that the hon. member for Laurier had read the report of the committee and would be familiar with what went on there. I am sorry he was not at the meeting at that time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister is quite right; I should have read the report of the committee. Unfortunately I was able to attend only the morning sittings, and I was unable to attend the afternoon sittings because of the debate on the civil rights bill which took place in the house. I was particularly concerned with the amendments upon which the pilots of the district of Montreal, Ottawa and Kingston made representations. I was wondering if, in his opening remarks, the minister could not give an indication to the house as to whether or not the government had acceded to those suggestions.

Canada Shipping Act
There were representations also made by the shipping federation of Canada, and it was upon those that I thought the minister might be able to give some indication as to what, in fact, those recommendations contained and why they were unacceptable, if that is the case, to the government. My object in asking for this information at this time is that once we get into a discussion of the clauses, then we are bound by the strict rule of relevance to discuss the clauses. I thought we should have this information now.
There is a third matter, however, which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. The minister will recall that when this matter was being discussed at the resolution stage we did not have the bill, and at the request of the minister we gave the bill second reading and sent it on to the committee in order to assist its passage, because I think there was general unanimity with its principles. This explains why some of us at least have not seen the bill since it returned from the committee.
I come back to my point. The minister will remember that at the resolution stage I asked him whether there had been any consultation with the pilots on the great lakes and what their views were. I have not the minister's words in front of me now and I would not want to misrepresent him, but my recollection is that there was no objection to any clauses of the bill raised by these pilots. Since the matter has been in committee I have received representations from the Canadian representative and business manager of the great lakes district masters, mates and pilots, through their captain. He states that to his knowledge at no time has the attitude of the pilots in the Port Weller-Sarnia great lakes district been sought. He suggests it would appear that, so far as the pilots in that area are concerned, they are not to be considered. His letter intimates that if the matter is not straightened out properly now, some day there will be serious repercussions.
There are protests which he makes, and I would ask the minister to allow me to put on Hansard those protests and then he can deal with them when he replies. I know he has received these protests, and I feel they should be brought to the attention of the committee at this time. These are the reasons given by the Canadian representative and business manager, Captain Norman S. Johnston, for his opposition to certain parts of this bill, and I quote from a telegram which was sent from St. Catharines on July 6, 1960:
X strongly protest the amending of the Canada Shipping Act in regards to the fixing of the number of Canadian registered pilots for great lakes pilotage service. All great lakes masters, with the necessary qualifications and experience, such as

three years as master or sailing master required by the ships' pilots' rating guide, should be registered and given equal opportunity and equal rights without discrimination of any kind whatsoever. This is their democratic right and privilege for equality of oportunity. Surely this will not be taken away from them in this great country of ours. When more pilots are required, as they are at the present time, they can be drawn from this inactive pool of registered pilots.
I further protest Department of Transport officials not honouring verbal agreement reached with them in Ottawa on January 29, 1960.
This is quite recent.
Among several things, the 50 hour work week as promised to the pilots' committee and myself on behalf of the Port Weller-Sarnia pilots who are prevailing rate of pay employees of the Department of Transport, is not being carried out. Pilots are criminally and inhumanly overworked in this area; 70 to 90 hours per week and more as government employees without extra compensation. This is not the fault of the pilot supervisor but of the D.O.T. officials in Ottawa who will not bring in sufficient pilots to relieve the pressure and nerve tension on those now working. This practice has been protested several times by myself to the officials in Ottawa as a representative of the majority of the pilots in this area. Surely this inhuman practice will not be allowed to continue. Apprentice pilots should also be given serious consideration in this pilotage area, especially on the larger vessels.
Then he adds a further protest that the circular entitled "Employee Group Relations", Department of Transport, is not being carried out by the departmental officials in Ottawa. He contends that by following this circular many of the injustices can be corrected. It would appear that if there were adherence to the conditions outlined in the circular, that would perhaps meet many of the difficulties that have been brought to the attention of the department.
Then of course, as the minister knows, Captain Johnston further protests the pilotage tariff as presently set up for the Port Weller-Sarnia pilotage district, which are perhaps the lowest pilotage tariffs in the world for this type of district. He says:
This is one of the most difficult areas in Canada and the world to manoeuvre and handle. Surely our pilots should not be criminally and inhumanly overworked to keep pilotage tariffs ridiculously low on behalf of foreign shipping interests when many more capable pilots are available.
I have not had an opportunity of discussing this with the business manager of the association since the first bill came up for discussion last year, and certainly I have not had an opportunity of discussing these matters with him lately. I put these protests on the record now and I would think, since the minister is aware of these representations, perhaps he might deal with them. I would also invite him as pilotage authority to ask his officers to see these people. I have found-as I am sure the minister has since he has been in office-that there is nothing like personal

contact in connection with these matters. If this group headed by Captain Johnston were given an opportunity to come down here and discuss these grievances, which on their face appear to be serious, I am sure that with the good will of the minister and his departmental officials they could be quickly ironed out.
Without dealing at undue length with these matters, I wonder whether, before we get away from clause 1-because it would be difficult afterward to come back to the general proposition-the minister could not briefly tell us what has happened to the representations made to the committee by the Montreal-Ottawa-Kingston district pilots, and next, what happened to the recommendations or amendments suggested by the shipping federation of Canada?

With regard to the last question asked by the hon. member for Laurier, may I say that a new subsection 3 was added to 375B as a result of the representations made by the representatives of the pilots at the committee meeting.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not in the bill that we now have before us. I obtained this copy from the table.

It is contained in the thirteenth report of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and reads as follows:
Clause 2
1. Page 2, amend the proposed new section 375B of the act by inserting therein immediately following subsection (2) thereof, the following subsection as subsection (3) :
"(3) Subsection (1) does not apply to a vessel registered in Canada or the United States
(a)	whose operations are upon the great lakes or between ports in the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river; or
(b)	whose operations are primarily as described in paragraph (a) and that makes occasional voyages to ports in the maritime provinces of Canada."
That was put in at the resquest, as I remember it, of the pilots who wished to have it made clear what ships were excused from requiring pilots by law. With regard to the telegram to which the hon. member from Laurier has referred-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before the minister moves on may I ask this question. Did I understand the minister to say that two amendments were made?

Yes. This is a proposal made by the committee for two amendments in new subsection 5 and new subsection 6 of section 375B. When we come to that I will read those proposed amendments and ask my colleague the Associate Minister of National Defence to move that those new subsections be added. If the hon. member for Laurier
Canada Shipping Act
wishes me to read those two new subsections now I shall be glad to do so, but I will do it at the appropriate time in any event.
With regard to what the hon. member said about Captain Johnston's telegram of July 6, may I say that I have here a report made to me by the chief of the nautical and pilotage division of the Department of Transport, as follows:
Captain Johnston in the telegram reiterates his complaint that the Port Weller-Sarnia pilots are being "criminally overworked".
The department never entered into any agreement with Captain Johnston, but at a meeting last January it was clearly explained to the pilots' representatives that the department's conception of a 50-hour work week was 50 hours of actual work on the bridge of a ship, and that it was on this basis that the salary was set at $1,200 per month. The pilots understood that they would not be considered to be working when they were asleep crossing lake Erie, or when they were waiting on a ship in port, doing nothing. Further, it was clearly understood that the 50 hours must be an average. Obviously they might be called on to do more than 50 hours in some weeks when traffic might be congested.
I checked with the supervising pilot at Port Weller on the present situation on Friday afternoon.
That was Friday during the first week of July.
I was assured that, counting the actual pilotage time as above mentioned, the average work week is less than 50 hours. He cited to me three or four cases in which the hours worked had risen to 53 or 54 in one week, but as against this there were many cases in the past month when the number of hours had dropped to about 20.
At the present time the pilots are having about two days off between trips and if they are complaining at all, it is because the time off is too long. They would prefer to be on board ship rather than sitting around a hotel.
The supervising pilot has received no complaints of overwork from any of the pilots and several of them have admitted to him that they "never had it so good.''
I might say to the hon. member that the pilots in this district are government employees. As he knows, there is a regular procedure laid down for approaches to be made to the government by such groups, and we are very glad and willing at any time to discuss complaints or grievances with them.

The bill as amended suits me and it suits our group. I pointed out in committee the difficulties that are inherent in these amendments. I think these amendments are all right, but this might be a very difficult act to get satisfaction from because of the relationships with the Americans.
I think Captain Johnston's wire, which I also received and which I took up with the minister, is indicative of the problem involved. This is a case where Captain Johnston is representing a remnant organization outside of the civil service to which the pilots have moved. But we have on the other side of the

Canada Shipping Act
line what is going to be far from a remnant organization; it is a very tough, militant United States union. All I can say is that I hope the minister has genuinely able, diplomatic people to run the scheme in association with the Americans.
From reading the report of the committee -and I was at quite a bit of the hearings- we find the amendments suitable. We hope the legislation goes into effect soon and works very well. The only warning I should like to make in connection with it is that if the minister and his officials do not play it fair and straight with the Americans, and perhaps in a more public way than they would normally tend to do, I think the legislation in some of its aspects is likely to collapse. For that reason I should hope that he would be perhaps even more open and that his officials would be even more open with the Americans in the processes, procedures and techniques of making this work than he is with members of parliament; because I think he is as aware as am I that he has a couple of very able stonewallers in his department. While it is all right to stonewall a member of parliament, and there is not much that he can do about it, if you start to stonewall United States people, especially United States unions, you may have considerable trouble.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister how clause 1 is going to apply together with the amendment which I now see is going to be made to 375D(5)? What I mean is this. This act apparently applies only from the international boundary line west. There is no division of the pilotage district as between anything east of the international boundary line in Canada and anything west. There is one pilotage district, namely the Montreal-Ottawa-Kingston pilotage district. Is it the intention to resubdivide that pilotage district so there would be a line, with all those west of St. Regis being in one district and those east-which would, of course, not be a very long distance-probably in the Montreal district? I have heard that said, and I wondered how clause 1 would apply.
The intention is to establish a new district from Montreal to St. Regis, and the remainder of the old district as far as Kingston is a question that is under discussion at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can the minister say what the name of the Montreal-St. Regis portion will be, and what will be the name of the new district west of St. Regis?
I am advised that the department has not decided on the name, but the division will be as 1 have outlined.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Can it be said at this time how the number of pilots will be divided as between the portion east of St. Regis and up river?
No, that has not been worked out; but I shall be glad to see that the hon. member for Laurier is advised when the decision is made, because I am aware of his great interest in this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask a final question in connection with the operation of clause 1 of this bill, arising out of what has been said by the hon. member for Port Arthur. I agree that great care will have to be taken in the negotiations which still remain to be completed between Canada and the United States. What strikes me at the moment is that one of the officers of the department, Brigadier Booth, I think, indicated in committee that many of the negotiations are not yet completed. These will have to be entered upon from time to time. Is it possible now to know which of the arrangements have been completed and which are still under negotiation?

I am advised that matters of detail still remain to be worked out. However, as the hon. member knows, there is a considerable period of time for these discussions still remaining. The discussions cannot be started on these details until both bills have been passed in the United States and in Canada. As soon as this bill goes through, if it does, these discussions will begin, and I feel confident that long before the opening of the navigation season next year all these matters will have been worked out. I hope they will be worked out by the middle of this fall.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister need have no worry about the bill not going through. I do not think there is any doubt about that. We all support it.
I never like to take parliament for granted.
Oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the amendment which is contemplated to the last section, that is 375B (5) and (6) but particularly (5), to be read concurrently with clause 1? In other words, is it the intention to make sure that the Canadian pilots are treated in the same manner as the United States pilots mentioned in clause 1?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. The whole purpose of this bill is to see to it that Canadian and United States pilots receive identical treatment, or as close as we can make it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Does that apply to the qualifications? That was the point.
The qualifications of the pilots in both countries are very similar indeed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

I believe that subsidies not only have played but are playing and must unavoidably continue to play a very important part in the railway policy and freight rate structure of this country. I am a little at a loss to know what the hon. member thinks of this measure. He has given it some very faint praise, and he has asked the government to keep it as a temporary measure. I want to tell the minister that I am in favour of this measure. We think, unlike the hon. member, that subsidies are going to have to play a very important part in the freight rate policy of the government and of the country if freight rates are going to be applied equitably across the country.
The hon. member says he believes in competition, and that competition will bring down freight rates. Competition may bring down freight rates in areas where competition exists, but since railways are absolutely necessary to the survival of this nation, then that kind of one-way policy without any subsidy means that in areas in which there is no opportunity for competition freight users will have to pay exceedingly high rates, extortionate rates. We on the prairies think we have been paying those rates, and I think the maritime people have been paying these extortionate rates, and for that reason we look favourably on this measure, just as we look favourably on other measures that will prevent increases in freight rates.
The hon. member said that a year ago I had made a statement-and he was critical of

I think that has been a good stand in the past. I think it is a good stand today.
The only thing I regret about this measure is that it has not been enough to roll back the whole of this 17 per cent increase in freight rates. However, it reduces it part way, between 7 per cent and 9 per cent, and to that extent I think it is a good measure. I hope this measure will pass the house, as I am certain it will, and that the royal commission may have the opportunity to report within the nine months' duration of this subsidy.
As has been pointed out, I said a year ago that I did not think a royal commission was necessary. At that time I did not think it was necessary because I felt that the government, on the basis of statements it had made in the past, should know the policies that it was necessary for it to follow. But since the government obviously does not know and since it needs a royal commission, then I think the commission is likely to do very good work, and I hope it will result, first of all, in at least the prevention of further horizontal increases in freight rates and second, in the bringing about of a more equitable rate structure in this country.

This item, of course, is perhaps one of the most important in the estimates of the Department of Transport, not so much because of the amount involved as because of the duties which have to be performed by the members of the air transport board.
I should like immediately to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Transport for his appointment of the new chairman of the air transport board. I think the minister has chosen well, not only because of the qualifications of the chairman but also because the appointment was well received by the industry. The committee will excuse me, I know, if I refer to the fact that the air transport board was established by perhaps one of the greatest public servants this country has known, namely Mr. R.A.C. Henry some years ago when he served under Right Hon. C.D. Howe, who was then minister of munitions and supply and afterward minister of reconstruction and supply, and under whose authority at that time fell jurisdiction over the air transport board. Mr. Henry was followed, I believe, by Mr. John Baldwin, who is now deputy minister of transport, and later by Mr. Matthews, head of the legal division of the department, now deceased, and now by Mr. Davoud.
I think the present chairman of the air transport board would want me to say a word also about those associated with him on the board. Able and qualified as is the Chairman, I think he is fortunate in having associated with him and to assist him two members who have had a great deal of experience, one of them almost from the outset. I refer to Mr. Dan McLean, whose experience in the field of aviation is known to all those who have been close to the industry. I am sure he must be of tremendous help to the chairman, to the board and to the minister. Last but not least I want to refer to Mr. Gerald Morisset, a former secretary of the air transport board, who has had a great deal 79951-0-405
Supply-Transport
of legal experience in the field of aviation, and who I am sure is of assistance to the board in its hearings.
I started out by complimenting the minister on his appointment of the chairman of the board. I regret that my remarks now are not going to be of such a complimentary nature. Of course I want to deal with the case of Georgian Bay Airways Limited which the minister on the bill of rights the other day, because of the charge I have made, tried to explain away, something which I do not think he was successful in doing.
I want to put on the record the application which was made by Georgian Bay Airways Limited for a series of flights into the Georgian bay area and other areas, which application was turned down by the air transport board. I hold in my hand now order No. 102, which contains a copy of the decision of the air transport board, serial No. 1359, decided by the board on December 1, 1959, denying the application of Georgian Bay Airways Limited for a licence to operate a charter commercial air service with group B aircraft.
I am not going to prolong this discussion. I am going to try to limit it, because I know it would be most unfair for the minister to spend an undue length of time on his estimates. 1 realize that he has already been here quite a long time. The normal time taken for the consideration of the Department of Transport estimates, in my time and since, I believe has been four days to four and a half days and sometimes five days. Examination of these estimates has already taken almost that long. Therefore I do not intend to labour the point unduly, though I feel I must bring this question to the attention of the committee.
The board gave a number of reasons for declining this application. The first was that Georgian Bay Airways Limited was attempting to expand out of the area which it had served for some years into a new area which up to recently had been well outside the scope of its operations. The decision continued:
The area which the applicant now desires to be licensed to enter has been served for many years by Austin Airways Limited and this company has built up over the years a service which in the opinion of the board serves the area adequately and is only now beginning to be operated on a reasonably sound financial basis. The evidence establishes that the applicant would generate very little new traffic and its proposed operations would depend therefore on traffic drawn from existing operators.
Later in its decision the board goes on to say:
The board is satisfied that the strengthening of Austin Airways' class 2 service is much more in

Supply-Transport
the public interest than the licensing of a class 4 group B carrier to operate at a key point on Austin Airways' regular specific point route.
And again:
In so far as the application for authority to operate with group B aircraft at South Porcupine is concerned, the evidence indicated no support for more than one group B aircraft at that point. Austin Airways Limited has been operating such a service for many years and to grant the authority requested by the applicant to operate a similar type of service at South Porcupine would impose heavy economic hardship on the established carrier and would not be in the public interest.
Finally, without going into additional detail, the denial of the application concludes with this paragraph:
In these circumstances the application of Georgian Bay Airways Limited for authority to operate the services set out in the title to this decision is denied on the grounds that the board is not satisfied that it would be in the public interest to authorize the applicant to operate these services.
So on December 1, 1959, the application of Georgian Bay Airways was declined by the board for the reasons stated. Then on January 15, 1960, the amendment to the order in council which had been passed by the previous administration, P.C. 2032 of December 22, 1954, was introduced changing section 6 of the commercial air service regulations and setting out that applicants for licences to operate commercial air services in all classes other than class 1 are exempted from the operation of subsection 3 of section 15 of the act provided that in substitution therefor applicants for licences to operate classes 2 and 3, group A of class 4, classes 5 and 6 shall satisfy the board that the proposed commercial air services would be in the public interest.
The air transport board found that this application was not in the public interest. That is point No. 1. The order in council amended the regulations on January 15, 1960, so that it would no longer be necessary to prove public interest. Then on January 21, barely one week later, followed a new application by Georgian Bay Airways for practically the same service, and this time the board granted the application in the light of the amendment to the regulations.
The minister replied, during the discussion on the bill of rights, when I said that this was done by order in council, that the regulations were changed under section 13 of the act by the former administration. Yes, that is so; and in reply to my question to the Prime Minister the right hon. gentleman said this was the kind of thing which was not going to happen again after the bill of rights had gone through.
The point on which I want to insist now is this; that the former government changed
[Mr. Chevrier.l
the regulations in the manner provided under the act, but they did not change them after the air transport board had decided against an application; they changed them by virtue of the authority given by parliament to the governor in council.
Here is a situation which is not on all fours with that of Autair-and I do not intend to develop that, because the minister has said that he intends to look into it and have an investigation. The situation I have described is as bad, and worse, because the air transport board declined after a public hearing to grant Georgian Bay Airways the various classes of commercial schedules which it sought. What the minister then did was this; instead of overruling the board, as he had the right to-although he would have been wrong in doing so, because this was a legal decision-in the same way as he did in the Autair case, he amended the regulations and then, in the light of the changed regulations, the air transport board had no alternative but to grant the licence. If that is not government by order in council, then I do not know what I am talking about.
'The air transport board held a full and careful hearing which lasted for some time. I have the evidence, and it is voluminous. As a result of that hearing the board decided that in the public interest this application should not be granted. Then, a month or more later, the board reversed itself and decided that the facilities sought should be granted because the regulations had been changed by virtue of the order in council I have put on the record. I think the minister owes the committee an explanation other than the one he gave during a discussion of the bill of rights; and I think, too, that the minister should tell us now who are the shareholders in Georgian Bay Airways Limited. With that information, perhaps we would be in a position to consider what the situation is.

At this time I might answer another question put to me by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, when he asked on July 13 how many commercial air transport companies were operating in 1957 and how many are operating today, how many aircraft they had and their categories, capacities, etc. In 1957 the number of commercially registered aircraft in Canada was 1,826. By the end of 1959 this had increased to 1,840. I cannot give the exact break-down as between types of aircraft, since this would involve a statistical analysis requiring some days to complete. I am informed, however, that the number of aircraft indicated for 1959 falls roughly into the following categories: 1,490 single engine, 195 twin engine, and 111 multi-engine, that is aircraft with four engines or more.
My point with regard to types of services is also substantiated by the following information. In 1957 there were 375 commercial carriers licensed in Canada; in 1960 the comparable total number is 496. In 1957 there were 87 carriers having group B licences involving 188 bases; in 1960 the comparable number is 87 carriers and 181 bases. It was under subsection 4 of section 15 by virtue of which, and I quote the subsection:
The board may exempt from the operation of the whole or any part of subsection 3, any air carrier or commercial air service or any class or group thereof, except a scheduled commercial air service operating wholly within Canada or the operator thereof either generally or for a limited period or

in respect of a limited area, if in the opinion of the board such exemption is in the public interest.
The point I make is that the order in council was passed by virtue of this subsection, and the board had decided that it was against the public interest to grant Georgian Bay Airways Limited the licence which it sought. The point I make now is that I have some doubt as to the legality of the position. I wonder whether the lawyers in the air transport board have given consideration to the legal status of this application. Is there a possibility that the position is a dangerous one for the department from the legal standpoint? There is no doubt in my mind that in this case, had the minister upset the board by way of appeal, an action would have laid against the crown. By circumventing the Aeronautics Act, as was done in this case, is the Department of Transport, is the air transport board open to an action in law? I think we should know.
I am informed that there is a serious legal position. The minister has not replied to the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in which he asked if it were so that John Bassett was one of the shareholders of this company. In addition, I should like to know if it is so that John David Eaton is a shareholder of this company. It also falls by the wayside in connection with the representations which were made by the air industries and transport association of Canada, which is worried lest the air transport board is going to have little or nothing to do hereafter. If the minister is going to continue to set aside decisions of the air transport board by appeal, or if he is going to continue to set aside decisions of the board by amending regulations under the Aeronautics Act, then what is the use of the air transport board other than to make surveys from one end of the country to the other to ascertain whether air services are required in one particular part of the country rather than another?
The air transport board was established under the Aeronautics Act to hear applications and here are two instances, the Autair case

heard at Montreal and the Georgian Bay case heard at Timmins, where the decisions were in effect annulled or set aside by action in the first case by the minister and in the second case by the governor in council. When the Prime Minister sat on this side of the house he protested bitterly with respect to that very kind of thing, that there should not be government by order in council. If it was felt that public interest was no longer a requirement, an amendment to the Aeronautics Act should have been made. The minister should have come into the house with a bill seeking to amend the Aeronautics Act, and should have told the house what the purpose of the amendment was. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps I misunderstood the minister. The minister says that the board operates in accordance with the policy of the government. I disagree with that. The board operates under the Aeronautics Act. It was established under the Aeronautics Act, and that is the reason it has been put there. While it is true that government policy is important, and that the air transport board must take cognizance of government policy, I come back and say that the minister had no right, because of that, to change a decision of the air transport board. The decision of the air transport board is made on a judicial basis. It is the minister who has turned that down. He is not a lawyer-and I do not say that in disrespect-but the point is that it was a judicial decision. This was the intention of parliament when this act was passed. The minister upset this decision, which was a judicial decision. The minister knows that the air transport board is a body which was established under this law and for that reason I submit, with deference to you, sir, that the minister was in error in changing the rules in the middle of the game.

I should like to ask the former minister, then, why his government put the stipulation in the Aeronautics Act that no licence could be issued without the authorization of the minister, and that any case could be appealed to the minister? Perhaps to settle this matter I might read again what I said in this house on July 7, as reported at page 5914 of Hansard:
As for the suggestion that the minister has assumed a role of interfering with the air transport board, I refute this completely. I have the

fullest faith in this board. It is my intent and practice to allow the air transport board to proceed without interference on my part to carry out its judicial functions under the Aeronautics Act in giving effect to the aviation policy of the government.
Subsection (1) of section 15 of the Aeronautics Act provides, however, that the board must have the approval of the minister for the issuance of a licence to operate a commercial air service; while subsections (9) and (11) of the same section provide that any air carrier has a right of appeal to the minister against the decisions of the board. These overriding powers granted the minister were inserted in the Aeronautics Act by the previous administration, presumably for a specific purpose; in fact, I assume the reason is similar to the reason behind the statutory provisions which allow a right of appeal to the governor in council in regard to certain types of decisions made by the board of transport commissioners.
It is my view that the minister should leave the air transport board a free hand in carrying out its judicial and regulatory duties, but that parliament, at the request of the previous administration, inserted these provisions in the Aeronautics Act which give the minister and the government power, if it should be his view and that of the government that the national interest requires the minister to exercise his special powers in regard to licensing policy in accordance with normal judicial procedure and with the law.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister asked me a question, is it not a fact that no licence could be granted without the approval of the minister? Of course it is a fact, because it is in the Aeronautics Act. This is not the point at issue. The point at issue is that the minister has just said, in quoting his remarks made earlier on the bill of rights, that he was going to leave the board free to act in carrying out its judicial functions.
He did not do that. That is exactly what the minister did not do, and that is exactly what we on this side of the house are complaining about. The judicial function of the board is to hear the application and, upon the evidence, determine whether or not it is in the public interest to grant the application. The air transport board said it was not in the public interest to grant the application in this case. Therefore the minister did not allow the board a free hand in a judicial matter, as the minister should have done.
What happened to make the minister change his mind? I think that is something that the committee should know. Repeatedly we have asked the minister whether these two persons Mr. Basset and Mr. Eaton are shareholders of Georgian Bay Airways Limited. The minister has replied that he cannot give that answer. I am not satisfied with the reasons he gave. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate put the matter properly. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and more particularly the board of governors, are required to give the names of all those who make applications. It seems

that this is something that could be done in the case of the air transport board.
However, the thing that is incomprehensible is that the minister says one thing in his statement and acts in a contrary manner. He says that he leaves the air transport board free in matters of a judicial nature. He did not do so in the first case, namely the Autair case, and he did not do so in this case. These are two matters of a judicial nature. Lawyers appear for and against the applicants. There are lawyers who advise the air transport board. There is certainly one lawyer, if not two of them, on the air transport board. It is a legal matter. It is a judicial matter. I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport what seems to be, in my opinion, a very serious anomaly in relation to the railway grade crossing fund. At the present time municipalities are not permitted to take advantage of the funds which are voted by the government for the elimination of level crossings when a grade crossing is built where there is no level crossing existing.
This case has been met with many times recently in Montreal, as for example in connection with a tunnel built under the C.P.R. tracks at Victoria street, another one under Masson street, and a bridge over the C.N.R. tracks at Dickson street, the three projects amounting to an aggregate cost of about $4 million. In order to obtain a grant it would have been necessary for the city of Montreal to have built three years ago a level crossing with all the inconveniences which such a 79951-0-406
Supply-Transport
measure would have entailed. Because the railway tracks in the city of Montreal form a complete circle, about the centre of the present area of Montreal, and because the population and inhabited territory are considerably increasing so that the streets have to be extended in nearly all directions beyond the circle, a number of other grade separations carrying the highway over or under the railway will still be required in the future.
The city of Montreal must accordingly, under the present provisions of the Railway Act, continue to pay such total high cost of construction of such grade separations, which will place a heavy onus on this already heavily encumbered municipality; or, in order to obtain aid from the railway grade crossing fund with regard thereto, construct a level crossing at a particular location and wait three years, at the risk of loss of lives and injuries, before constructing the immediately required grade separation.
The city of Montreal is therefore suffering a serious prejudice in this respect, and unless the Railway Act is amended to allow for construction of grade separations where there is no existing crossing, such prejudice and heavy burden will continue to increase.
Such an amendment, in cities where the situation is the same as that now existing in Montreal and in provinces where industrial development is closely associated with highway improvement, would tend to increase the claims upon the fund. In order to lessen such an increase in the claims upon the fund, such amendment could allow a contribution therefrom to be made wherever the crossing involved an arterial highway, being a highway constructed to carry a main stream of traffic, which was crossing or was being crossed by a railway.
May I add that an over-all program of railway grade separations in such a way as to bring improvements where they are most needed first and then, in a given period of time, throughout the whole country, is the only way to bring an efficient solution to a problem which has been plaguing us for the last 50 years. The board of transport commissioners should have the power and means of establishing such a program and of deciding on priorities of execution according to their surveys and analyses, without restrictions as to dates and pre-existence of the road.
The present government has initiated the most daring effort ever made by any government toward an efficient solution of the railway crossing problem. I take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Transport for having taken this initiative. May I suggest to the minister that intensive research be initiated toward finding a way of relieving

Supply-Transport
the municipalities of a financial burden which is worsening their already bad financial situation, by integrating entirely these undertakings of grade separations within the national development program of our great country, and thus ensuring the implementation of an efficient program of railway grade crossing elimination within a reasonable period of time to the great benefit of our always expanding nation.

I should like to make a very few remarks with reference to the alarming situation regarding the removal of train services. I think that we, as members of the government of Canada, should join in a common purpose, a common understanding and a common program to keep the railroad industry healthy and thriving, and to face those in the industry who seek to consolidate the nation's railroads into a few noncompetitive systems under the guise of efficiency and economy.
It seems that their objective is to get maximum profits even though it means denying the public its rights of convenience and necessity. I feel that the railroads are attempting in some cases to neglect their passenger and freight service so that it will show a deficit, and thus make it easier to apply for the removal of trains and trackage, thus having an adverse effect on the people and the small businessmen who have located on these lines.
It is my honour, Mr. Chairman, to represent a riding the people of which through the years have had to depend largely on the railroad for their transportation and the delivery of their daily needs and commodities. Also in this riding is the town of Havelock, a railroad terminal centre, which for many years has depended on the railroad as its major source of income. Knowing intimately many of the railroad employees throughout the riding, may I say that these men believe in a bright future for the rail industry. They are ready to stand shoulder to shoulder with enlightened management and the government in order to assure that future.
Surely anyone with the foresight and vision of the future shown by the Prime Minister would readily agree that within the next few years our population will be at least tripled. We should bear in mind the European countries, with their dense populations who depend almost entirely on rail commuter service to and from the metropolitan areas, and to the most distant suburban centres, as being a public service.
It is my opinion that the management of our railroads must assume a good deal of the responsibility for the decline, to some extent, of passenger and freight loads. As an

operator of a small business may I say that many times representatives of the transport trucking firms have called at our place of business soliciting business for their firms and inquiring if we had any complaints or any suggestions as to how we thought the service could be improved. Yet never once over many long years were we called upon by representatives of the railroads, and never did we have the courtesy of a letter thanking us for past business or soliciting new business. Is it not evident who is responsible for the decreasing traffic?
However, at this point let me say that from my experience of the years during which I have travelled on the railroads I cannot too highly praise the train crews. They are most courteous and they have done, and still are doing, all that is in their power to create good will between the railroad and the passengers who use it. Management could surely take a lesson from such men.
I should like to see a study made of the number of employees who had been released by the railways in Canada during the past year and the effect this has had on small businessmen and the economy of the communities concerned.
In closing, may I predict that railroad passenger business will revive and grow, providing more jobs for railway workers, and that it will be a far more efficient service for the public than ever before. This can be attained provided a high quality of dedicated leadership is shown. May I say, Mr. Chairman, to the minister through you, that I plead with him and his department to give this matter his very earnest consideration, because it is one of utmost importance which affects every Canadian and the country as a whole.

I should like to make a brief comment and say that the hon. member who has just spoken has struck a very responsive chord in my heart. I was pleased to hear a representative of the Progressive Conservative party criticize the railroads for considering the maximization of profits before service to the people. I was pleased, also, to hear him attribute some responsibility for the decline in traffic to the kind of service which is being given in some places and also to hear his plea, if I understood him correctly, for an enlightened approach by management.
I associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member who has just spoken and I should like to tell the minister, also, that the representative of Kootenay West and the employees of the Kettle Valley railroad are willing to sit down with management to try to find a solution to this question which will

be sound and satisfactory to the people concerned and which would provide the service that is necessary.

Perhaps I might call attention to an aspect of this question particularly in terms of the commuter service between Truro and Halifax. Each year more of this service is being abandoned by the C.N.R., and I think it should be drawn to the attention of the management that there is a point of public relations involved here. If they are not going to satisfy passengers on the short hauls by providing an efficient service it becomes increasingly difficult to impress on those people that they can provide other services.
I know the C.N.R. is trying to reshape its public image, and I think places such as commuter services in areas which are expanding, such as the Halifax metropolitan area, would be very good places in which to start before running to the board of transport commissioners to ask leave to abandon services of the type I am considering.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On this item I think the minister should give us some indication of what is happening in the maritime commission at the moment. There is a new chairman, Alex Watson, an old and trusted employee of the Department of Transport, who for many years was in charge of the icebreakers in the St. Lawrence and who, I am sure, because of his experience, will fulfil the post of chairman of the maritime commission well. But I think the minister owes it to the committee to tell us what is happening. There are two additional members and I believe they come from other branches of the department. One is, I think, the director of the economics division of the Department of Transport and another, I am inclined to think, is also a departmental officer. That may be the right policy in the circumstances, but I think we should be given some idea of the duties of the commission. I do not want to get into a contentious field as I did a while ago with regard to airways. That is not my intention, but the minister will recall how critical of the maritime commission the Secretary of State for External Affairs was, when the hon. gentleman was on this side of the house, after it had been established. I shall not repeat that criticism because I did not agree with it at the time but, of course, when the commission was established there was a practical need for it. Does that need still exist?
There was also a large number of other duties, including work in connection with 79951-0-406J
Supply-Transport
steamship subventions. I assume they have not decreased. Perhaps, indeed, they have increased. There were other matters. For example, the minister had a certain freedom to grant permits to ships under foreign registry to be registered under the Canadian flag. Can the minister give the committee an idea how many of such permits have been granted under the special powers which he possesses? Perhaps I should stop at this point.

Regarding the personnel of the maritime commission, as the hon. member has said the chairman and two commissioners are new. The chairman is now Mr. Alex Watson and he is assisted by Mr. George Scott, assistant deputy minister, economics policy branch, Department of Transport, and by Mr. John Rutledge, director of shipbuilding in the Department of Defence Production. As the hon. member for Laurier knows, the two departments with which the maritime commission works are the Department of Transport and the Department of Defence Production. The two gentlemen I have just mentioned in addition to acting as commissioners on the maritime commission act as liaison between the commission and their two departments.
The main duties of the Canadian maritime commission are to co-ordinate the administration of shipping matters and recommend to the government policies for preservation of the shipping and shipbuilding industries. The commission is authorized to investigate and study Canadian requirements with respect to shipping services, Canadian shipbuilding and ship repairing facilities, and the costs of building ships in Canada and operating them under the Canadian flag.
With respect to shipbuilding, it is commonly recognized that Canadian shipyards suffer from high cost of production, exceeding costs abroad by from 20 to 50 per cent or more and, in addition, plant capacity is probably greater than normal Canadian needs at the present. As a means of meeting this problem the government has followed and the industry has benefited from measures designed to assist in securing commercial orders as well as from orders for naval vessels and vessels for other government departments. At the present time, due largely to a substantial drop in bookings of commercial work, the order volume is less than for several years past and average employment in the major yards has declined. This situation is under review by the commission and I am hopeful that remedial measures will soon be brought forward for the government's consideration.
With respect to the operation of Canadian deep-sea vessels the government has

Supply-Transport
continued the policy of permitting registration of most of them in the United Kingdom to reduce the high cost associated with Canadian-based operations. While this has been of some measure of value, the Canadian deep-sea operators continue to be at a competitive disadvantage because they face a higher tax liability on their earnings than do United Kingdom operators, who are granted a special exemption, the investment allowance, intended to assist them in meeting competition from ships sailing under flags of convenience with small tax liabilities although the number of such Canadian owned vessels continue to decline as war built vessels are retired. It is nevertheless true that under this policy some firms have acquired new vessels and likely will continue to operate them.
Canadian domestic operators may be divided into three groups each having somewhat different problems. Those in the Atlan-tic-St. Lawrence trades face much the same difficulties as the deep-sea operators as a result of competition from vessels on United Kingdom registry. In these trades Canadian registered vessels perform most of the scheduled services but carry comparatively little of the bulk cargoes. Many of these Canadian operators use chartered United Kingdom vessels. On the west coast the situation for coasting vessels is basically different in that the operators experience little or no competition from United Kingdom operators and almost all of their vessels are registered in Canada. On the great lakes the St. Lawrence seaway now admits oceangoing vessels to compete with the specialized lakers, but it will take further experience to demonstrate whether or not the well established Canadian lake fleet is at any serious disadvantage.
In addition to the tasks taken on by the Canadian maritime commission they handle coastal shipping subsidies. For many years the federal government has subsidized a number of shipping services in coastal and inland waters. The services are deemed to be essential but are not self-supporting. Subsidies are considered to be warranted when, at a reasonable cost, they make possible a dependable transportation service which is necessary for the supplying of outlying communities.
The administration of the subsidies is a responsibility of the Canadian maritime commission. The commission receives applications for subsidy assistance and makes its recommendations after investigation of the circumstances, and it reviews the subsidy requirements with the operators each year in the light of experience. The adequacy and

the efficiency of the services are investigated regularly, and the financial results are exam-mined in detail to establish the need for continuing government aid. In some cases the service may qualify for provincial assistance too, and this is taken into account. The amount of the subsidy is established on the basis of the actual loss incurred by an operator in performing the service, including allowance for an acceptable return on invested capital.
The commission and the Department of Transport make economic studies from time to time to assess developments or trends that may affect transportation requirements and the need for subsidies. The result may be a recommendation to modify, curtail or abandon a subsidized service, or to withdraw the subsidy in favour of encouraging an alternative service.
The subsidy program is given a careful review by the treasury board each year, which must satisfy itself that each payment is justified. To this end the board may direct that studies be made of alternative services in a particular case or within a given region.
I will give the committee the picture regarding coastal subsidies up to this year. These subsidies are up this year to just over $6 million, an increase of about $600,000 compared with the 1959-60 fiscal year. Transfers to the United Kingdom registry under the transfer plan were 11 during the 1959-60 fiscal year.

May I ask the minister a question on this steamships subvention item. I notice that the subvention for the western local service is $294,000 out of a total of $6,088,200. We have our problems and they
Supply-Transport
are serious ones. I do believe they are trying to resolve them on the west coast. I refer to the provincial government and also the services. In view of the fact that the companies operating are losing as much money as, if not more than the people on the eastern coast, I do not understand why the subvention on the western coast is approximately $700,000 out of a total of almost $7 million. Will the minister explain the policy on the granting of subventions?

Mr. Chairman, as I indicated
earlier, each service stands on its own feet and subsidies are paid only where there is an actual operating loss by the shipping company concerned. Each case is reviewed every year and stands on its own merits. If the service is necessary and is losing money, then that is given very serious consideration by the maritime commission and the government in the paying of a subsidy. The actual operating losses incurred by the shipping companies which are supplying services on the west coast are obviously not nearly as great as those suffered by the companies supplying the service on the east coast. In each case the government tries to see that necessary services are provided for the people of the areas concerned.

Is this policy carried out without discrimination? In other words, if the Black Ball ferry service in British Columbia loses money would the company get a subvention? This is what I should like to know. If the two new government ferries of British Columbia lose money will they be entitled to assistance from the minister's department?

Any shipping company can make an application but it would have to make a case that would be satisfactory to the maritime commission and then to the treasury board. First of all, it has to make a case that it is an essential service and second that it is losing money.
If it is an essential service and is losing money, whether privately owned or publicly owned, the department will consider paying a subvention?
Another factor that is given very real consideration is whether or not there is any other form of transportation available to the citizens concerned.

They felt that this is just the kind of thing that should be done more often; personal discussions should be held between officials of the government and

Will the minister tell us whether out of the $1,876,000 for Quebec there is anything for the improvement of the highway called, I think, Petit Champlain?
