Mr. Chairman, as I said a moment ago, the part played by Montreal harbour in the economy of this country and of the Montreal area does not seem about to decline in importance.
During the last generation, the industrial function of the harbour has become increasingly evident, so much so that today two thirds of the port's activities of which depend upon industrial production of the area in which it is located and the expansion has barely started. In fact, almost 75 per cent of all incoming traffic is meant for the Montreal area while close to 50 per cent of the harbour's outgoing traffic is supplied by the neighbouring territory.
With the rate of industrial expansion in the district of Montreal, the harbour remains an excellent transshipment centre, where the already well-established regular shipping lines prefer to operate. With those well established regular shippings lines, with its harbour facilities continuously kept up to date and especially with the growing importance of the surrounding industrial complex, the harbour's industrial usefulness must

necessarily increase also, with consequent maintenance or growth of its commercial function.
While Montreal harbour activities depend very largely on industrial production in the Montreal area, conversely, the area's development depends to a large extent on the volume and efficiency of its harbour traffic. In fact, today, Montreal's economic future is bound up with that of its harbour.
Montreal harbour is now undergoing extensive renovation, and in recent years almost $60 million have been spent on improvements to harbour facilities. Sheds, wharves and other facilities have been put in, or are now being built to meet the harbour's new requirements, especially those called for by the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway.
Yet who would claim that such developments have nothing to do with the physical development of the city itself? One would have to be blind to deny that the Montreal harbour cannot be physically dissociated from the rest of the city. We need only look at the roads leading to the harbour to realize that they were designed for other times and other modes of transport than those in use today.
There can be no doubt, therefore, about the need for integrating with the harbour's development the proposed east-west throughway planned by the city of Montreal along the St. Lawrence. Between Place Royale and Notre-Dame-de-Bonsecours church, elimination of obsolete buildings would make room for the throughway and, at the same time, provide space for harbour requirements in the area where that space is most needed.
In the same way, the network of large traffic arteries in the city must be adequately connected with the harbour's approaches and parking facilities. In this regard, the lack of parking space in the harbour area has often been pointed out. Longshoremen alone park more than 500 vehicles a day in that area.
This lack is keenly felt by longshoremen and other harbour workers. The longshoremen who, during the shipping season, often have to work 18 hours on end, and sometimes more, cannot find places to park unless they get there an hour ahead of time, thus cutting down their hours of sleep. Many times, through lack of parking space and of time, they have to park illegally and pay fines,
Supply-Transport
with consequent loss of income. This deplorable situation calls for immediate remedy, and I hope that the Minister of Transport will see that a solution is found, even if only for a time. However, conditions there are unquestionably a cause of trouble and annoyance to harbour workers, especially to longshoremen, whose role is so vital to the smooth operation of the harbour.
Nobody can deny that the industrial development which has taken place in connection with harbour operations in the city of Montreal and in the surrounding areas will also be streamlined and stepped-up to a degree unknown for several generations. That industrial growth will require functional development in the newer parts, and redevelopment in the older ones. In such development due regard must be had for road and railroad networks, industrial needs, shipping facilities and proper use of available sites.
One case in particular that cannot be ignored is that of the Lachine canal, which offers a typical example of the changes gradually brought about by the development of the local economy, especially in relation to the harbour and shipping. The Lachine canal is no longer being used by sea-going ships bound for the lakehead. It is becoming merely a service waterway for industries already established along its shores. There is no doubt that a transformation must take place during the next generation in the use of the industrial area bordering on this canal.
Therefore, the development or re-development of the Montreal shore of the St. Lawrence requires an over-all plan that will take into consideration the needs of the harbour and of the city, determine the needs of increased industrial occupation, and provide, as of now, for the necessary measures with respect to traffic, free areas and land use, so that full advantage can be taken of the industrial growth of that area and of the first-class harbour facilities now available.
Definitely, the problem cannot be solved by a mere study of the needs of the harbour or of the city, but only through a combination of efforts on the part of the authorities concerned. It is high time Montreal harbour should stop being considered as a separate entity, severed from its physical, economic and social context. Harbour authorities have as much interest in the industrial development of Montreal as have municipal authorities in the development of the harbour.

Supply-Transport
There is a further aspect to the problems created by the St. Lawrence seaway and by the development of the Montreal harbour, which the Montreal metropolitan area cannot ignore without suffering serious consequences.
The very site of the St. Lawrence seaway, south of Laprairie basin, and the presence of cultivated land in the neighbourhood of the 35-foot channel north of Boucherville, are bound to require extension of harbour facilities on the south shore of the St. Lawrence.
In the area of Varennes, Vercheres, Con-trecoeur, gigantic Canadian and American firms have already built plants representing an investment of hundreds of millions of dollars. They include the Steel Company of Canada, Canadian Titanium Pigment, Electric Reduction Co. of Canada, Quebec Iron Ore, Shawinigan Chemicals Limited, and a number of oil companies. A number of steel manufacturers, such as the Steel Company of Canada, Dosco and Quesco have also invested several millions of dollars in that area. The steady additions of new docks near the shipping channel in that area raises important problems for the future, to such an extent that official consideration should soon be given to extending the limits of the Montreal harbour right through to Sorel. Thus the harbour facilities at Contrecoeur, Varennes and Vercheres, and related industries would become physically linked to the port of Montreal, and their development could be planned with that in mind.
It is to be hoped that the Montreal harbour internal planning committee, which was set up on the initiative of this government, will give consideration not only to shipping problems but also to the problems of urban development in relation to the development of the river shores.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) has said that the report of that committee will be available shortly and that the study will include a very extensive and thorough examination of the joint possibilities offered by the development of harbour and industrial facilities in Montreal harbour and its future extensions. I wish to commend the Minister of Transport for his excellent move.
There is another related problem from the standpoint of needs, and I refer to a bridge in the eastern Montreal area.
This changing pattern on the south shore, from agricultural to residential and to industrial, reflects on the physical development of the whole metropolitan area, a phenomenon is causing a complete change in the feeling prevailing so far that the Montreal metropolitan area did not extend beyond the
[Mr. Campeau.l
limits of the island. Today, from an economic standpoint, Montreal's insularity is an obsolete concept. It is in that sense that it becomes necessary and urgent to multiply means of communications between both shores and that it becomes economically justifiable to do so, for the proper integration of the whole metropolitan area and to link it to the mainland.
Montreal island, having ceased economically to be an island, must be linked with the south shore by as many bridges as are required over the St. Lawrence.
It would be a very shortsighted policy on our part to base the necessity for a bridge in eastern Montreal solely on surveys of the present volume of traffic and to assess on that basis the need for a bridge and the possibilities of financing it. Those who think that way overlook the fact that in the matter of development we must take into account direct and indirect benefits, as well as appreciation in increased values created by physically indispensable facilities.
The eastern part of Montreal island is rapidly developing at both the industrial and residential levels. It therefore offers an increasingly large labour market for existing and proposed industries on the south shore.
Because of the rapid growth in the eastern part of Montreal island and on the south shore, building of a bridge at that point across the St. Lawrence is as vital and urgent as the completion of Nuns' island bridge, because of the development on the territory around Candiac and Laprairie, and of the proposed renovation of the western sector of Montreal city.
According to many experts, the most suitable location for that bridge seems to be through Ste. Therese island, between Pointe aux Trembles and Varennes, thus connecting metropolitan boulevard, Sherbrooke and Notre Dame streets and the proposed east-west throughway along the St. Lawrence river with the south shore highways leading to Quebec, the eastern townships and the United States.
This bridge would link the south shore industrial development with residential and commercial centres in the eastern part of Montreal island. A bridge there is therefore essential to the industrial development of the area and to the growth of the harbour. Moreover, it will provide a vital link between the active part of Montreal harbour on the island of Montreal and the section now under

development along the south shore. For that reason, a bridge to the east is obviously essential, and there is no need for traffic counts that reflect existing economic conditions, but fait to take into account those that will come to light when necessary facilities will exist.
A good many people worry about the means of financing this bridge. It seems that all levels of government have a direct interest in this project. First of all the federal government, for the functional development of the harbour; the provincial government for the completion of its regional road network and the promotion of the steel and iron industry; and the city of Montreal and its metropolitan area for the progress resulting from such developments.
Among the necessary steps to develop Montreal harbour and the neighbouring areas, there is one which cannot be stressed enough, and that is the deepening of the Richelieu, giving the channel a uniform depth of 35 feet between Montreal and New York, that is the same depth as the St. Lawrence downstream from Montreal.
The new Ruhr already taking shape on the south shore in the district of Varennes, Ver-cheres and Contrecoeur, lends this project an urgency and significance which many people could hardly grasp until recent years.
That river of the scenic shores is the present route for the transport of newsprint required by the large American newspapers. However, in a not too distant future, the Quebec iron and steel industry will be in a position to offer its products to American buyers.
We must immediately open this natural seaway to New York and to the eastern United States, the most industrialized area in the world.
The project is much more simple than it would seem at first, especially when compared to the St. Lawrence seaway. A reliable estimation of the cost places the total expenditure in the neighbourhood of $185 million for the Canadian section. The money saved by using this water route would make up for this expenditure in a relatively short time. Consideration must also be given to increased land values alongside the waterway, as a result of the possibilities for new industrial development in the Longueuil and St. John districts. In fact, there is extraordinary interest, from a shipping point of view and from an industrial point of view, in providing for two channels on the south shore, one leading to the sea, to the centre and western parts of the country, and the other to the sea and to east central United States, with Montreal harbour at the strategic meeting point of both.
Supply-Transport
In concluding, Mr. Chairman, may I emphasize the fact that economic development in the Montreal area is directly related to the growth of its industry and of the harbour, and that it offers considerable possibilities. However, necessary steps must be taken at the proper time to offset the disadvantages and to make the most of the favourable factors.
What is needed is the necessary vision to find an over-all solution to the major problems connected with Montreal harbour, its facilities, its relations with the surrounding area, the roadways, the railway system and the bridges spanning the river. There must be a well-defined master plan for the harbour, integrated with the orderly development of the surrounding area.
The planning for Montreal harbour must be on a grand scale, and I feel sure that the Minister of Transport who, in the past, has displayed considerable interest in that harbour, will continue to concern himself with its progress and will press for the early carrying out of such essential projects as the construction of a bridge in eastern Montreal, the development of a Richelieu waterway and the rational improvement of both the harbour and its future extensions.
Finally, consideration should be given to the need for large scale public works in the Montreal area, where the workers are so directly affected by unemployment whenever a slowdown occurs in private business.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one question to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees).
Could the minister inform the house whether a project is now under consideration for the extension of Montreal harbour facilities, both on the south shore and on the north shore, towards eastern Montreal?

speechtext: Order. May I say whether it is the wish of the committee to discuss items 456 and 493 at the same time in order to avoid confusion?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
In that case I suppose the hon. member for St. James, who first rose, should have the floor. I have no objection.

Supply-Transport
Yes, Mr. Chairman, we have under consideration at the present time an extension of the limits of Montreal harbour downstream possibly to the limit of Sorel harbour.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that I could not allow the remarks made by the hon. member for St. James to pass unnoticed. It is not that I disagree with what he has said; on the contrary, there is very little of what he has said with which I would find myself in disagreement. There are, however, some things of which I believe the committee should be reminded because the hon. member for St. James now takes a somewhat different view from that which he took on an earlier occasion.
The hon. member will recall that he was very critical of what has been done by the former administration concerning the port of Montreal and the surrounding metropolitan area. In fact, he took me to task very severely because of the fact, when I was president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, I had done nothing for the city of Montreal and everything for the city of Cornwall. However, his colleague who sat next to him, the hon. member for Stormont, said I was doing nothing for the city of Cornwall and everything for the city of Montreal. I believe these two hon. members should get together and try to agree as to wherein lies the truth.
Although I find myself in agreement with the hon member's other remarks, there are some things which should be brought to the attention of the committee. The hon. member for St. James referred to an amount of something like $60 million that had been or was to be spent on the port of Montreal. I suggest it was my successor Mr. Marler who announced an expenditure of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $100 million for port facilities in the city of Montreal, the most of which I understand have now been completed, in part by the former administration and in part by the present government. This is all to the good. It is, of course, unquestioned that this port development has been brought about as the result of industrial development in the triangle formed by Valley-field, Sorel and Montreal. They are owing in large part or in no small part to the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway.
In the first years in my capacity as minister of transport I remember that when I brought to the attention of many Montrealers the importance of this development there was great anxiety and perhaps rightly so. There was also some fear that this develop-

ment might affect and hurt the port of Montreal. I do not want to speak out of turn because, in my opinion, it is yet too early to determine whether the over-all effect is going to be beneficial. However, of one thing there can be no doubt, namely that in the season of 1959 as well as in so much of the season of 1960 as we have come to thus far there have been great benefits which have arisen out of the St. Lawrence seaway for the whole metropolitan area of Montreal.
There is also no doubt that it is because of the lower transportation costs that the steel industry, to which my friend the hon. member for St. James refers, finds it convenient, and profitable and strategic to locate itself in the area of Contrecoeur in the area east of Montreal. But as I said, I do not want to anticipate what is likely to happen. I think it will take several years-maybe three, four or five years-before the ultimate benefits of the St. Lawrence seaway can be felt in certain areas and regions of Montreal and more particularly in the port at Montreal. There was a prominent Montrealer who not long ago made the statement in the province of Ontario that no province in Canada would benefit from the St. Lawrence seaway more than would the province of Quebec and more particularly the city of Montreal. Thus far the facts seem to indicate that such is the case.
I should like to say a word now about the report which was made by the Montreal harbour committee and which I have discussed from time to time. The hon. member -for St. James-and I think rightly so-speaks of a study which was made concerning future developments. The 1950 report on the Montreal harbour was made by five prominent engineers. They recommended a definite plan for development dowstream of the city of Montreal which amounted to about $100 million following upon the development of the seaway. I think the study the minister is making is all to the good. However, I am hopeful that the minister will give consideration to the report of the 1950 committee. It might be well to bring that report up to date.
It rightly provided for certain lock facilities, the construction of a bridge east of the Jacques Cartier bridge and several other matters that would be necessary consequent upon the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway. However, that report was predicated upon the fact that the St. Lawrence seaway was to be built on the north side or on the Montreal side. As the committee knows the seaway, because of necessity-and I think rightly so-was built along the south side or the Laprairie basin side. The recommendations made by the 1950 committee are still not up

to date but they should be considered as part of any study which the minister is making.
There is no doubt in my mind-and on this I am in complete agreement with the hon. member-that there is a necessity for an additional bridge east of the Jacques Cartier bridge. As to its location, I have already said that I am not competent to say where it should go. That is perhaps a matter for others to determine. The point I should like to bring to the attention of the hon. member for St. James is that the Minister of Transport is not of the same view as are he or others who have advocated the construction of this additional bridge. I do not want to become contentious once again but I draw to his attention the correspondence which the minister had with the municipalities on the south shore wherein he indicated some serious doubt as to the additional bridge. He did this notwithstanding the fact that the associate minister of national defence is also a strong advocate of the bridge. The minister's statement is long. I shall read only one paragraph which can be found in sessional paper No. 170E of February 29, 1960. In his letter to the reeves and mayors of the various cities and municipalities of the south shore we find the following:
I am informed that a most careful analysis of traffic trends and related statistics indicates that when the new bridge is completed-
He is referring to the Champlain bridge.
-the capacity of the three bridges should be in excess of actual requirements for a considerable number of years. Any new bridge presumably would have to be financed through tolls and would divert additional traffic, and thus it seems inevitable that substantial deficits could be anticipated for quite a long period of time. This indicates to me that regardless of other considerations, the course of wisdom for whichever authority may assume responsibility would be to wait at least until the effects of the new Champlain bridge can be examined before undertaking the very substantial financial outlay that would be involved in the construction of yet another bridge.
There is a serious question mark in the mind of the Minister of Transport in connection with this additional bridge. We all know that the population of Montreal has increased. We all know that the automobile population on the island of Montreal has gone up tremendously. We all know that there is a great need for an additional bridge. I made a suggestion some two years ago in a motion that I placed on the order paper to the effect that a crown corporation be established which would have the control of the Jacques Cartier bridge, the Victoria bridge by purchase or by lease from the C.N.R., the new Champlain bridge and any other bridges that might be built east of the Jacques Cartier bridge; and that that crown corporation after having
Supply-Transport
looked at the picture, which would indicate that soon the debt of the Jacques Cartier bridge will be completely wiped out if the same policy is followed as was followed in other national harbours, namely to wipe out the interest debt, might come to an agreement with Canadian National Railways. It would appear then that it might be good policy to give to the new crown agency the duty of constructing the new bridge in question. I think that is a matter which might well be given consideration.
My friend the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres is unavoidably absent. If he were here I know he would want to say a word in connection with the development of the lake Champlain cut-off. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because the Prime Minister went down to Sorel and by his presence there, without committing himself to the project but by his very presence there at the request and at the invitation of certain public bodies certainly must have created the impression that something was going to be done. Nothing has been done. There has been a request to the Canadian government by the United States government to set aside a sum of money for an economic study of the whole lake Champlain cut-off from Albany right up to the St. Lawrence river. I understand the Canadian government has not responded to that request. It is one thing to say this looks like a good project, tbut it is another to act upon it and undertake to set aside money for an economic or engineering study.
Then again there is the all-important decision of the international joint commission arrived at, I believe, in 1937. At that time the international joint commission, having given careful study to the lake Champlain waterway, stated that until the St. Lawrence seaway was completed it be authorized to retain jurisdiction over the matter, but after the seaway had been completed such a study should be made. I had no intention of speaking on this subject, but in view of what the hon. member for St. James has said I think the minister should tell us, first, whether the international joint commission has been asked to consider the possibility of these studies and, second, what has been the attitude of the Canadian government to the request by the United States government for a sum of money to enable a survey to be made from the international border to the St. Lawrence river on the economic and other aspects of the Champlain waterway.
These are things which those of us from the province of Quebec and the metropolitan area of Montreal are keenly interested. The first and foremost matter is that a study

Supp ly-Transport
should be made. For the best study which could be made it would be well to follow the pattern initiated in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway, namely that it should be a joint one, because half of the project is in Canada and the other part is in the United States. More progress would be made if the study were conducted in this matter.

A preliminary review is being carried out at the present time by the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. When the preliminary hearing has been completed the results will be considered by my department and the Department of External Affairs and we shall know what more detailed work is needed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the minister dealing now with Richelieu or Montreal?

I thought the question which the hon. member asked dealt with the Richelieu project. With regard to his question of Montreal harbour, the Montreal harbour planning committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Paul Kuring, the retired head of the ship channel branch, is bringing the original study up to date. Participating in the study are the national harbours board, the C.N.R. and the Department of Transport.

Can I ask a further question of the minister? I do so because this is the only opportunity I will have to ask a question regarding expenditure in the riding which I represent. There is no other department which spends any money there except the Department of Transport. I have no public works.
Certain people accept that the inner harbour of the city of Vancouver is one of the major ports on the North American continent and that it has a great future. It has been said that in the inner harbour on the south side, from Hartley avenue, where the hon. gentleman was a couple of days ago opening the Centennial pier, up the Boundary road, lies the greatest potential for the future development of that harbour. I should like to ask the minister whether there is any planning going on in his department for the further development of the inner harbour and expenditure in connection therewith. The places I have mentioned are the southern boundaries of my constituency.

I am advised that the Vancouver harbour standing committee is at the present time reviewing the question which the hon. member has just raised. As the hon. member probably knows, this committee is making a study of the whole of Vancouver harbour, and the section which he has mentioned forms part of that study.
That work is now going ahead?
Yes, the study is going ahead and I can agree with the hon. member regarding everything he said about the great potential of Vancouver harbour.
And of the Vancouver east section?
Undoubtedly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am rising at this point to draw the attention of the minister to a matter concerning the harbour of Vancouver which was consistently brought to the attention of the committee from year to year. I hold in my hand now a release from the ministry of transport dated October 6, 1959 which announces:
To further the development of Vancouver harbour the national harbours board have announced a study of present and future needs of this great harbour by a committee-
And so on and so forth. Of course, there can be no fault to be found with that, and I am not rising to find fault with it, but I am rising to remind the minister that the Secretary of State for External Affairs lost no opportunity when he was on this side of the house to recall the terms of the Gibbs report and to ask me why it was an advisory committee of the port of Vancouver was not established and consulted and its advice sought. Each year there was a debate which lasted, sometimes 35 or 40 minutes, in connection with the establishment of advisory committees not only in Vancouver but in most national harbours. As far as I can recollect the only harbour which has one- and I may be mistaken-is Halifax, where they have a port committee. But I cannot resist the temptation of asking the minister why he did not consult his colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs before he made this announcement.

The setting up of this committee at the time it was set up seemed to be a progressive and logical step to take, and as this government always takes progressive and logical steps, that is why we did it.

A number of years ago one of the finest piers we had in Vancouver, the Canadian Pacific railway pier, was ruined by fire and it is now burned out. I should like to ask the minister whether he or the national harbours board have any authority whatsoever to order it to be reconstructed or put to use in any way. That location at the foot of Granville street is one of the finest locations that there is anywhere in the world, and I was wondering whether the

minister has any authority to move in and order planning and reconstruction to take place.

One of the reasons why we went ahead with the building of the Centennial pier was that the C.P.R. indicated they were not proceeding with the rebuilding of that bumed-out pier. In the whole study of Vancouver harbour now being undertaken such suggestions as the hon. member has made with respect to this burned-out site will be given serious consideration by the government. This whole matter is under study at the present time.
If the considerations do not result in action, has the minister or the government any authority to order that this fine pier location should be utilized?
No, Mr. Chairman, not short of expropriation.

Items agreed to.
Air services-
491. Acquisition of land for control of properties in the vicinity of main terminal airports to prevent the erection of hazards to flying and for future development of new and existing main terminal airports including alternative facilities for relieving congestion thereat, $3,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a brief moment to ask the Minister of Transport about a matter which I know he regards as important and which I certainly think is highly important in the constituency I have the honour to represent, and that is the airport at Windsor and its future prospects and development.
The minister will remember that he had the honour, which I envied him, of formally opening that airport shortly after the election of 1957. The hon. gentleman was gracious enough on that occasion to mention that the preliminary work had been done by his predecessor. He was also gracious enough to give me an opportunity of participating as one of the members in the district and I want to publicly thank the minister for that. The hon. gentleman showed qualities of real understanding of the vicissitudes of public life in the way in which he accorded me, as one of the members in the district, the opportunity of participating in that very happy ceremony.
We are very proud of that terminal. I think it is one of the finest in the country if not the very finest, possibly second only to the new terminal in Ottawa. I would think the terminal in Windsor is among the two finest in the country and second only to the one in our capital.
The air transport business is not all that we would like it to be. I am not blaming the
Supply-Transport
government or anyone for that. I should like to know from the minister if he could tell us what the prospects are in this respect. At one time we were hoping that C.P.A. would run out of Windsor to Mexico. It seems to me that Windsor is so located that there ought to be the greatest encouragement given to airlines from other countries to use these terminal facilities, particularly if one bears in mind how close Windsor is to that great United States city of Detroit.
There are quite a number of people at the Windsor airport whose employment is vitally affected by this situation. I would think with the potential growth of the city of Windsor and its particular locale opposite the city of Detroit it would lend itself to very great air development. I would be very grateful to the minister if he could say something that would confirm my own hopes in the matter and those of my fellow citizens generally.

The land requirements of the Windsor airport are under review at the present time to ensure that we have all of the land that we need for any future expansion. There is no immediate runway expansion planned but this expansion will be undertaken if it is needed.
Regarding increased requirements by commercial air lines, if we receive notification by any commercial air line that they have an additional requirement for length of runway or anything of that kind I can assure the hon. member and other hon. members for the Windsor district that we shall certainly see that we do not lag behind in providing for Windsor the facilities needed to make it possible for air fines to increase their services to that very important city.
During the present year there is improved lighting going into the airport and road improvements as well representing an expenditure this year of some $60,000. I should like to conclude by telling the hon. member that we agree with him that this is a very important airport serving a most important city and that we will not lag behind in any way in providing the facilities needed to allow for the expansion of the use of that airport.

Could the minister tell us what is the reason for the delay in C.P.A. being able to undertake its Windsor-Mexico run? I have been in touch with the president of that company who informs me that it is not because of any fault in Canada, that the delay has occurred in Mexico. That would be one additional means of giving further activity to the airport. Could the minister comment?

S upply-Transport

I am advised that earlier the Mexican government would not allow this agreement to go into effect. At the present time, however, there is no application before the air transport board by Canadian Pacific Air Lines to re-open negotiations. I can assure the hon. gentleman that if we do receive an application from C.P.A. to re-open the negotiations we shall be very glad to do so right away.

Mr. Chairman, I apologize to the minister and to the committee if the hon. gentleman has already made a statement with respect to this item and my question arising from it. Would the minister tell us what is the policy regarding requirements at the Vancouver international airport? All air traffic is consolidated at that airport including commercial flying, private flying, R.C.A.F. flying and international air traffic. The minister's predecessor and the present minister have both had under consideration an alternative airport for this area. Will something be done or will private flying continue there? Has the Minister of Transport consulted with the Minister of National Defence about the speed of defence aircraft, and the problems relating thereto? I appreciate that there has been much consideration and consultation but I think there has also been much vacillation and I should like a clear answer from the minister. Can the minister give us some clear indication-I may be on the borderline of being out of order, Mr. Chairman-of his attitude toward the new consultations having to do with the taking over of the Vancouver airport on a commercial basis?

Yes. As I understand it, the people of Vancouver wish that the satellite airport should be in the Boundary Bay area. I have carried on discussions with my colleague the Minister of National Defence and have urged on him strongly the need for the Department of National Defence to vacate that area just as soon as possible so that we can move in and take it over as a satellite airport.
Do I understand that this has been agreed to by the R.C.A.F.?

No, it is an installation of the Department of National Defence at the present time, as I understand it. As soon as the Department of National Defence will move out the installations which are holding us up, then we shall certainly move in and take over Boundary Bay.
I am sorry; will they move in and take over Boundary Bay as a flying field?
I am sorry; I did not catch that.
On what basis are you going to take over Boundary Bay?

We are going to take over Boundary Bay provided that national defence move out. We still have available the Pitt meadows site and if we find the delay is going to be too long and that the Vancouver area is not willing to wait, then we shall be very glad to develop the Pitt meadows site. We are still hopeful we may be able to develop the Boundary Bay site. I appreciate what the hon. member has said about the desirability of getting on with the job; I agree with him. I am just as anxious as he is to get on with the job.
With regard to the taking over of the Vancouver airport from the municipal government of Vancouver, I have had discussions with them recently about that. Representatives of the municipal government of Vancouver will be in Ottawa a week from today to start discussions on this matter. I have indicated that this government is perfectly willing to take over and operate the Vancouver airport. All that remains is for a mutually acceptable price to be agreed upon regarding the facilities owned at the present time by the city of Vancouver. Once that has been agreed upon we can go ahead and develop the airport.

May I ask a
question supplementary to the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Will the minister comment on the policy of his department with respect to aid to municipalities under this item in so far as airport facilities are concerned. In the past the policy has been to encourage wherever possible the municipality to participate in the erection and the running of facilities, whether they be airports or air terminals. However, more recently we have seen, as an example, Vancouver and a number of other municipal airports in Canada being taken over by the department or completely constructed or the facilities purchased. I could cite some other examples.
In my own city of Calgary the municipality has entered into partnership with the Department of Transport and under this arrangement has carried on a very successful utility. Of course, the government made a substantial contribution toward the facilities of this airport. Still more recently we have seen cities such as Edmonton and Ottawa, and now Vancouver, where the government has undertaken all the functions of commercial and civil aviation at those airport terminals. My purpose in raising this question is this. It must raise some doubts in the minds of the municipal councils to learn that after they

have entered into a partnership and undertaken substantial construction costs themselves the government has offered substantial grants and undertaken completely the operation of airports without any participation of the municipality concerned.
I think the first policy was sound in that obviously if you get a municipality which has an interest in the undertaking or the air terminal it puts some civic spirit into it and, of course, reduces the amount of money that the public treasury requires to put up. Latterly we seem to be going in the other direction, where there is too little encouragement to the municipality to operate as a partner. Therefore, one looks back and wonders whether it was a wise decision for any municipality or city to undertake a large financial responsibility, as was done so often, in view of the fact that conceivably had they waited a little bit longer they might have had the entire undertaking removed from them by the Minister of Transport. Will the minister comment on that?

I think I can answer the hon. member's question by the following statement of policy. The present arrangement under which the majority of airports are federally operated, particularly in the secondary field category, is the result of historical development and wartime growth. Basically speaking, however, the present policy is that the federal government encourages municipal operation of airports, and at main line airports served by scheduled services may, if necessary, pay a subsidy to a municipal airport operator to meet operating deficits. If the municipality is not prepared to operate the field and if the field is a major airport required to carry out international commitments, the federal government would assume responsibility.
In other cases, particularly requests for construction of a new airport, the federal government normally requires municipal participation giving as a minimum assurance it will provide the land for the air field and agree to operate it after the federal government has constructed it. In the case of local airports, dollar for dollar participation may also be required. The granting of operating subsidies to meet municipal deficits are dealt with by special investigation, both technical and economical, in each case and then a reference is made to treasury board for decision.
I might say with regard to the particular airport in which the hon. member for Calgary South is interested, namely the Calgary airport, that the Department of Transport is very pleased indeed with the way in which the city of Calgary has operated the airport.
Supply-Transport
They have done a first-class job; they have built a first-class air terminal building, and run it in a very commendable fashion. We are very happy to have municipalities carry out operations of that kind. However, as I said, if at any time a municipality decides that it does not wish either to construct or operate an air terminal building, then the Department of Transport is willing, as we are doing in the case of Vancouver at the present time, to discuss the value of the facilities owned by the municipality with a view to taking them over; and if an agreement can be reached between my department and the municipality regarding the value of the facilities, then we are willing to take them over and continue operations under the Department of Transport.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have a question about the Cornwall airport. I remember some money was in the estimates several years ago for that municipal airport. I wonder what the situation is?
I am advised that the application is dormant. There has been no application from the city for quite some time; also, there has been no application from any air line to use Cornwall as a port of call.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is the point. I wanted to mention to the minister I saw in the press Friday that the new airport is now almost completed and will be ready for operation soon. In the press also appeared the statement that Wheeler Air Lines and Quebecair had given indications that they wanted to apply to the air transport board for a milk run from Montreal to Toronto by way of Cornwall, Belleville and other places. I now hold in my hand the application which was made to the air transport board for the right to operate between such places as Montreal, Cornwall, Kingston, Peterborough and Toronto with the restriction, of course, that no through traffic from Montreal to Toronto or in the other direction would be allowed because that would be interfering with the licences of C.P.A. and T.C.A.
But in the Montreal Gazette of July 15 there appeared a notice of withdrawal by Quebecair Incorporated of an application for a class 1 licence and of its submission of a new application for a class 1 licence, which application is for the same service except that Cornwall is being dropped. My purpose in rising was first of all to ask the minister if he would inquire from the air transport board why Cornwall was contained in the first application and is being dropped in the second one.
I would also ask the minister to give consideration to assisting the municipal airport

Supply-Transport
at Cornwall because unless there is some service such as would be provided by Wheeler Air Lines or Quebecair it will be impossible for the airport to survive. I know that when I was on the other side we introduced a vote in the estimates, pending negotiations with the municipality, and did so on two occasions. I should like to know whether consideration will be given to an application if it is made.

As the hon. member for Laurier knows, having been minister of the department in the past, it is up to the air line concerned whether or not it will apply for certain ports of call. I will be glad to ask the air transport board if they have any information with regard to why Quebecair dropped Cornwall as a suggested port of call and will let the hon. member know, but whether or not an air line applies for any port of call is up to the air line itself. I can assure the hon. member that if an air line applies to stop at Cornwall we will take into consideration the needs of that air line from the point of view of landing strip length and other facilities that would be required. We will certainly not be backward in looking after Cornwall in the same way that we do in the case of any municipality when a scheduled air line applies to use that municipality as a port of call.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the application have to come from the municipality or from the operator of the airport?

I am advised that the municipality would approach us first and indicate to us that a certain air line intended to make the municipality a port of call. I understand we would then check with the air line and would have to receive a specific application from the air line. In addition, the municipality would then have to agree to acquire the land and operate the airport.

I should like to put a question to the minister if it has not been put in my absence. Some years ago a survey was instituted in the St. John's area to find an alternative out Topsail way for the airport at Torbay. Could the minister bring us up to date on the survey?

I am afraid no alternative site to Torbay has been found. There was a survey but we still have not been able to find an alternative site and the search is still going on. If anybody has any suggestions we will be very glad to look at them.
I am glad the minister has said that because I am sure this will be published in the St. John's papers and he will get more mail from now on.
I shall be glad to read it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to mention a couple of matters that I wish to bring to the attention of the department. At the present time we only have the two large airports at Vancouver and Calgary with practically nothing in between to handle the aircraft that are being developed at the present time. I suggest that more assistance should be given to the smaller airports in the interior of British Columbia. We have small airports at Penticton, Castle-gar, Cranbrook, Kimberley and Creston. Until such time as we are able to develop a larger airport in the interior of British Columbia I believe the smaller centres should be given some assistance, especially in the Kootenays, so as to protect the larger aircraft travelling west from Calgary and east from Vancouver.
At the present time there is no protection at all for the large aircraft now in use and the larger aircraft anticipated in the future. At the present time several airports are being developed in a small way by municipalities in the east and west Kootenays and if some assistance could be given to developing these airports to a greater extent it would afford tremendous protection for aircraft travelling this route because I feel that soon or later we will have to develop a major large airport some place in the interior of British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to support briefly the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay East and to suggest that by improving the Castlegar airport we would achieve greater advantage for the people of the district by the expenditure of the money required than by following any other course of action at the present time. We cannot foresee the future but developments are taking place very quickly and the building of a larger airport could be carefully studied over a period of time.

Item agreed to.
Canadian overseas telecommunication corporation-
492. Loan to the Canadian overseas telecommunication corporation in accordance with section 14 of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation Act for additions and betterments to facilities, $17,000,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this vote has to do with the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation, and I should like at once to commend the board of directors of that crown corporation for the excellent annual report they have submitted to parliament. I believe that much of the credit for that goes to none other than Mr. D. F. Bowie,

the president of Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation. I am particularly interested in this matter for two reasons. First, it was the former administration that introduced the bill setting up a crown corporation to expropriate Cable and Wireless and Canadian Marconi and also to build a submarine cable with a large number of circuits from Canada to the United Kingdom. The former administration was also responsible for the construction of the new building in Montreal. Therefore I am happy to see how well the corporation has carried on and how successful it has been in its operations, more particularly with respect to the balance sheet. That was the first purpose that prompted me to rise.
The second purpose is that I have received a number of inquiries concerning a contract given by C.O.T.C. and I wish the minister would help me with them. He may not have the information with him now but I trust that he can get it. I will put these questions on the record with an explanation of the reason for asking them. These are the questions to which I should like to obtain answers: Were tenders called for the laying of the submarine cable between Newfoundland and Iceland, called Icecan? Who tendered for this cable: what were the names of the tenderers and their prices? To whom was the contract awarded? Will a submarine cable be laid between Canada and Australia? What is the cost thereof and how will the cost be distributed? What percentage will be Canadian? Now what is the purpose of these questions? The purpose of these questions is that I have received considerable criticism by way of correspondence concerning the granting of this contract. I am told, and I will be corrected if I am wrong, that the contract has gone to a foreign corporation. I am told also that representations were made to the government by a French firm which had submitted a tender and which manifested a desire to start an industry at Three Rivers in the province of Quebec. I am sure this will bring the circumstances to the attention of the minister. I am informed also that this firm has spent considerable sums of money in buying land in that area and was prepared to establish a Canadian subsidiary. It would be in a position to construct this cable and was prepared also to employ no less than 300 people in Three Rivers. I am informed this is a substantial and reliable firm which already owned the land I mentioned, which land I am informed amounts to 2,500,000 square feet.
I am also informed that the government was advised that this company was willing to come here and establish itself in that area, and also to open an electronics industry
Supply-Transport

Quite some time ago, I think it was at least two years ago, I was visited by representatives of the French company to which the hon. member referred. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Here I should like to say a word in connection with the new appointment which the minister has made. The minister announced in the house some time ago the appointment of a new president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority who was the former vice chairman of the national harbours board. I know Mr. Rankin; I have had the pleasure of meeting him. No one is happier than I with regard to his appointment.
However, I think I should tell the minister that he is going to lose the services of a great public servant in the person of the present chairman of the St. Lawrence authority who has been in office in various capacities, beginning in the Department of Finance, continuing in the national harbours board and now with the St. Lawrence seaway authority, for I believe almost 40 years. I think the people of this country as well as

the committee would want me to pay him the tribute which he so richly deserves on this occasion.
I hope the minister will not mind if I, in a closing comment, say that I think the government is missing a great chance in not availing itself sufficiently of the services of the other member of the St. Lawrence authority, namely Mr. Jean-Claude Lessard. I may say frankly that here is a man who has trained a large number of people in the Department of Transport, particularly in the economics branch. He knows more about economics than do most of those who are now in the minister's branch. He trained most of them. He is an expert in the economics field. He has a degree from Harvard University. He has had a great deal of service not only as an economist in the board of transport commissioners division of the department but also as deputy minister of the Department of Transport except in so far as air services were concerned. He is a man who is rusting in the St. Lawrence seaway authority, whose talents are not being used, and who is a great public servant.
I ask the minister to give consideration to that matter. I will not say what I intended to say but I hope the minister will find it possible with regard to this public servant, this man who I think is full of sincerity, to make the use which should be made of the training he has received not only in the Canadian National Railways and at Harvard, but in various other transportation fields.

I read over the 1959 financial report of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. I note that it contains a report on the cleanup of construction on the St. Lawrence division and also the operation of the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals under that authority. I notice that there is a sum of $13.9 million outstanding in contractors' e'aims. I should like the minister to make some comment and to say how these claims were settled.
I might say that in order to expedite the passage of ships through the Welland canal some tie-up walls were built and the minister at one time in the house stated that they would cost $12 million. At another time I heard that they might cost $7 million.

If I may, I should like to correct the hon. member. I am not aware that I ever said that they would cost any more than $7J million, I think it was. That was the first estimate. We are very happy that they cost considerably less than that amount.

I should like the minister in his reply to tell me exactly what they cost. I know that the costs of the canals were to be amortized over a period of 50 years.
Supply-Transport
In the case of the Welland canal I believe the cost of deepening was in the neighbourhood of $29 million. Costs of the Welland canal were made up of the cost of operation plus the cost of amortization of the $29 million or whatever the cost was over 50 years. I was just wondering how the minister was dealing with the cost of the tie-up walls and whether the amount was added or whether it is to come as a separate vote.
I do not intend to deal with tolls. I have dealt with them several times previously in the house. However, I just wanted to raise one question. When the Welland canal was taken over by the St. Lawrence seaway authority as of March 31, 1959 the municipalities along the Welland canal were told that they would be treated in the same way as they were treated by the Department of Finance in respect of the Municipal Grants Act. These municipalities, of course, provide all the services to the canal. On two or three occasions in the house I have spoken on these services and I will not cover them now. However, I thought I would give you some break-down of the Municipal Grants Act in my town.
There the Welland canal has about 69 per cent of the taxable acreage and slightly over 2 per cent of the building assessment. They pay about 10.03 per cent of the taxes. I am told that in determining the grants the seaway authority will not be taking into consideration the evaluation of the buildings on the canal property. I turned up the Municipal Grants Act, section 2, paragraph (c) which reads as follows:
(c) "federal property'' means real property owned by Her Majesty in right of Canada, but does not include . . .
(iii) an improvement to land or structure that is not a building designed for the shelter of people, plant or movable property-
I know there is a double negative in there. I know there will be no people living in these buildings. However, it includes plant in so far as there is movable machinery; and this machinery can be moved. I have seen it moved. Payment was made up to and including March 31 by the Department of Finance, and in that payment the department took into consideration the value of buildings.
About two weeks ago I wrote to the minister because no cheque had been received in respect of the period between April 1 and December 31. Since that day they have received a cheque. I have heard from other municipalities, and one other municipality at least claims that it has not received anything from the St. Lawrence seaway authority with respect to that period from April 1 to the end of the year. In its payment to Thorold the seaway authority did

Supply-Transport
not take into consideration the value of the buildings. In the previous three months the Department of Finance did. In my small municipality that makes a considerable difference and I would think that a post office or any federal building would come under the definition of land improvement. Why should the Department of Finance include payment in respect of these buildings and the St. Lawrence seaway authority not? I have nothing more to say except that the municipalities are upset because some of them have received no payment in respect of last year's taxes and this year some of those who have received taxes are getting smaller grants than they had expected and budgeted for.

I can assure the hon. member for Welland that the city of Welland has been paid up to last year. Referring to the grant for the current year, negotiations will proceed between the authority and the municipality with a view to working out an amicable settlement as has been done in the past. The hon. member asked why the grant to certain other municipalities had not been paid. If he could mention the names of those municipalities I would be able to give him an answer. I understand from the chairman of the authority that most of these municipalities have been paid and that the remainder will be paid in the near future.
I understand that the grant for Welland has been paid, but does the authority intend to pay grants in respect to buildings or not?
I am advised that this is a matter of opinion in specific cases and where those cases come under dispute we obtain legal advice and follow that advice.
Can I ask the minister a specific question about the administration building in Cornwall? Would the authority pay a grant in lieu of taxes in respect to that building?
Yes, a grant in lieu of taxes would be paid.
Would it not apply to other buildings?
I am advised that that depends on what the building is used for.
Is that contained in the Municipal Grants Act?
Yes, I am sure the St. Lawrence seaway authority follows the principles laid down in that act.

I should like to know why for three months we were getting taxes in respect to the buildings along the canal and

then for the nine months after which the seaway authority took over we got no taxes in respect to those buildings.

I am advised that the St. Lawrence seaway authority interprets the act differently than did the canals branch of the Department of Transport. If the municipality of Welland feels it is not receiving a square deal I assume there is a perfect right to take the matter to the courts.
Is that not discriminatory on the part of the seaway authority toward these municipalities?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is one question I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and I think I owe it, in fairness to those who are now in the seaway authority, to do so. It concerns an article which appeared in the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder of July 14 entitled: "Condemn Land Condition Iroquois to Cornwall". I make this intervention with due apology to the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas, but I know she would be the first to deplore these conditions. A statement is reported by Reeve Lloyd Davis of Iroquois that nothing had been done to clear huge mounds of dirt from the lock area and beautify the site. According to this report, Reeve Davis termed the condition there as scandalous.
I am not asking the minister for any information now; I am just telling him what happened. When the seaway authority decided to expropriate Iroquois point it required to get the consent of no one, but in order to keep the peace with all concerned we obtained the consent of the council, and the three members of the authority went to Iroquois and dealt with them, and one of the stipulations or terms was that a park would be made of the area south of the lock at Iroquois and it would be beautified in the same way as was done at Cornwall. These people were then quite happy. Apparently, that promise has not been kept.
I know that when there is a change of government the new government is not obliged to keep promises such as that, though this was not a promise; it was rather more than a promise, it was an undertaking. I am sure that as a result of the statement I have made the members of the St. Lawrence seaway authority will wish to see that what was undertaken by the previous members of the authority is carried out in this case, and I ask the minister to be good enough to say that it will be done.
I shall certainly be glad to look into that.

Mr. Chairman, before making any comments on the estimates before us I should like once more to congratulate all the employees of the Department of Public Works upon the magnificent work they are doing and upon the devotion with which they fulfil their respective duties. The services they render to the country are deeply appreciated, I am sure, by every Canadian. I should also like to assure them that any criticism which may appear in my remarks is levelled not at them but at the government which is responsible for the department's policy.
It is generally recognized, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion of the public works department's estimates becomes more orderly as we proceed with consideration of the various items. For that reason I shall confine myself to certain general remarks and reserve the right to make any necessary comment later as the various items are submitted.
We all remember the sarcasm with which the former minister of public works, when his estimates were under consideration in June 1958, accused the former government of padding that department's estimates with projects it had not the slightest intention of carrying through. He added that for the year 1957-58 about 97 per cent of the allotments had actually been spent as against 91.7 per cent for the preceding year which was the last complete year of the Liberal administration. On June 4, 1959, speaking on the same estimates, I showed, with figures to prove it, that for the first full year of the present administration, that is 1958-59, only 89.5 per cent of the amounts allotted had been spent. I pointed out to the then minister, in passing, as a reply to his taunt, that he had not been able to keep his pace very long and had soon become winded.
Has the situation in that respect improved during the last fiscal year, that is 1959-60? For my own information I have prepared a table indicating the amounts voted, including statutory estimates, and the amounts spent during the same year. An analysis of this table shows that out of a sum of $226.5 million voted in the main and supplementary estimates, only $208.9 million was spent. This last figure appears on page 65 of the budgetary papers brought down by the Minister of Finance on March 31st of this year. It is arrived at by subtracting the $6.3 million for the national capital commission from $215.2 million.
Supply-Public Works
At first glance one might be inclined to think that the total amount represented by unfinished projects during the year 1959-60 is equal to the difference between the sums voted and the amount spent. In fact, Mr. Chairman, there must first be subtracted from the amount of expenditures $4 million, the difference between $52 million and $48 million. I think last Friday the minister used the figure $53.2 million but that does not change the final result. I repeat, there must be subtracted from the amount of expenditures $4 million, the difference between $52 million and $48 million, for the trans-Canada highway, which is a statutory expenditure, and $1.1 million paid to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This leaves $22.7 million unspent or approximately 10 per cent of the estimates.
The difference between the expenses foreseen in the estimates and the amounts actually spent during the year 1959-60 is even more apparent in an analysis of the following items. First, with respect to public buildings, construction and services, out of a total amount of $33.7 million voted for the acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings in centres other than Ottawa the sum of $27.8 million was spent or 18 per cent less than had been foreseen. Second, under the heading "Harbours and rivers engineering services", out of a total amount foreseen of $44.7 million the total expenditures amounted to $35.9 million. In this instance the difference is of the order of 20 per cent.
Therefore I feel justified in calling the attention of the minister and of hon. members of the committee to the fact that during a period when unemployment had reached a new high, the government, a supposed champion of full employment, instead of spending the amounts voted by parliament at its request and which should have been used for public works has considerably reduced its expenditures.
Furthermore, a simple analysis of the estimates as submitted by the Minister of Public Works for the years 1958-59, 1959-60 and 1960-61 indicates that far from increasing as they did under the former Liberal administration the department's estimates have been falling off from year to year which offers a great similarity to the government's popularity which is also showing a rapid decline. In fact, the estimates voted for the year 1958-59 were $233 million and the money spent was $220 million. In 1959-60 the estimates voted were $226 million and expenditures, $203.8 million. For the current fiscal year the minister is asking us to vote $195.9 million which is $25 million less, if we compare this year's main estimates with last year's.

When the house took recess at six o'clock, I was saying that the government has pitifully failed to perform its task with respect to the public works projects it intended to launch to provide jobs for the unemployed.
If the minister wants additional facts in support of my statement, I shall be pleased to provide them, taking them this time in the province of Quebec.
He must no doubt remember the visit he paid in early January of this year to Quebec city where, surrounded by his Conservative friends and supported by his parliamentary secretary, he predicted with typical eloquence and enthusiasm, a wave of prosperity that
Supply-Public Works
would provide Quebec people with more jobs and help relieve unemployment. His statement was published in the January 12 issue of L'Action Catholique.
He also stated on that occasion, as reported in Le Soleil for January 12:
The amount of money spent on public buildings in Quebec in 1958-59 was 27 per cent higher than the average spent in the last two years of the Liberal administration. Work on the new postal terminal in Quebec, which is estimated to cost $3 million, will start in early spring. In addition, in this very constituency, we are considering the construction of a new building for the unemployment insurance commission. An amount of $500,000 was included in the last estimates for that building.
Well, let us see what happened in the province of Quebec concerning the construction of public buildings since 1958-59, the first year for which the Conservative administration introduced its estimates.
For the fiscal year 1958-59, $12,007,000 were voted for acquisition, construction and improvements of public buildings.
For the fiscal year 1959-60, $5,931,000 were spent for the same kind of projects, which means a decrease of over 50 per cent as compared to the previous year.
For the present fiscal year, 1960-61, it is proposed to spend only the tiny sum of $3,673,000, which means a decrease of 70 per cent as compared to the year 1958-59 and $6,287,000 less than in 1956-57, last full year of the former Liberal administration.
Well, the minister must realize that if we continue at that rate, there will come a time when not only there will be no more public buildings erected in Quebec, but even the necessary repairs will not be taken care of.
The wave of prosperity which he predicted for our area will certainly not be due to the projects his department proposes to carry out this year. However, if there is a province and a city that are affected by unemployment, they are our province and the city of Quebec, where, on April 21, 1960, there were 17,546 people registered at the national employment office.
I therefore suggest to the minister that he hasten the drawing up of plans and specifications for the future unemployment insurance building, about which nothing was done last year, in spite of the $500,000 earmarked for that project.
As to the new post office building which has just been started, I think it my duty to point out that the government does not deserve to be commended for its speed as regards the project, because it took exactly three years from the time the work was started.

l should like to say a few words now, Mr. Chairman, about the possibility of building a causeway across the strait of Northumberland. It will no doubt be recalled that in 1958-59 an amount of $360,000 was voted for the examination of that project and that last year an additional amount of $250,000 was requested for the continuation of the study. This year we are asked to approve another vote of $50,000. Consequently, it seems that under the circumstances, and after having approved those expenditures, members of the committee are entitled to more information than they have been given up to now.
The minister will recall that when he made his statement on Friday last there was not a word in it about this important project. In view of all the important things that were said in that connection during the last federal election and, even more, during the provincial election in Prince Edward Island last summer, the minister should tell us what commitments have been made by the federal government and what assurances have been given to the new premier of Prince Edward Island who, as we know, was greatly helped in his election by the promises he made in regard to the causeway.
It will be recalled that during the provincial election in Prince Edward Island the people were asked, through the use of much advertising, to vote for the Conservative party which called itself the party of the causeway. Up to now, except for a few remarks by the former minister of public works and the present minister of that department, very little information has been given in the house to show us or at least to give us an inkling that it is economically possible to implement this project. The only way we could get information concerning the project was by reading the preliminary report which the deputy minister made in Charlottetown but which was refused to the house. A perusal of that report shows that various government departments and various firms of consulting engineers have carried out the following studies:
1.	The effects that such construction could have on the high and low water levels through the strait and the damage that could result to private properties and harbours.
2.	A land survey to determine the location of the waterline on the shores.
3.	An estimate of the damage to private properties and of the cost of protective works.
4.	A study of the formation and movement of the ice.
5.	A site survey to determine which location would be most appropriate for the construction of the causeway.

6.	Soundings across the strait.
7.	Two lines of borings across the strait to investigate foundation conditions.
8.	Borings and analysis of the stone of various neighbouring quarries to determine whether a sufficient quantity of stone is available and whether it is of such hardness and size as to make its use possible.
9.	Preparation of preliminary designs for the various types of construction which could be considered.
Since the department has all this information at hand, I feel that they can estimate the approximate cost of that project and say whether or not it would be economically possible to implement that project. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the results of the studies and research which are being carried out at present will only slightly affect the estimated cost of the causeway. Unless it can be proved without doubt that I am mistaken, I am inclined to feel that the deputy minister's visit to Prince Edward Island to present the report was intended to prepare the people of that district for the burial of that project for several years to come.
Other people seem to share my feeling since, according to a Prince Edward Island newspaper, many of those present when the deputy minister read his report were of the opinion that the completion of such a project would be in the far distant future, probably not within the life span of many of those who attended the meeting. The people of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island will have to realize that its famous project which was advocated by the Conservatives was merely another of the numerous visions of the Prime Minister.
