Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in connection with this socialist enterprise, the Department of Public Works. I must say before commencing that the department has established a record that has not been equalled in recent years. The department is headed by a master mariner, who showed that his feelings have always been close to the water when he used the simile the other day that we shall now enter the pacific waters of public works. The deputy minister is a general who is in command of batteries in Operation Avalanche which are in permanent position, firing at the same target in perpetuity and whose enemy returns every spring, requiring annihilation all over again. Never before in Canadian history has this happened.
I must say that I appreciate the minister's personal attention to the representations I have made to him on behalf of my constituents. I have appreciated his promptness 79951-0-407
Supply-Public Works
in dealing with correspondence; that he was willing to listen to my pleas, although I must say there have been occasions when he has not reacted as favourably as I hoped. I am rather forgiving in that respect because I understand that the treasury board is the ghost behind the scenes these days.
I should like also to express to the deputy minister my appreciation of his attention to my suggestions and pleas on behalf of my constituents concerning matters I have brought to his attention as a result of my own observations of the Department of Public Works in my own constituency. I cannot go on without extending my sincere congratulations to the deputy minister upon being presented with the engineering institute's Julian C. Smith medal for achievement in the development of Canada, which medal I understand was presented to the deputy minister at the 74th annual meeting of the institute in the Royal Alexandra hotel, Winnipeg. I mention that because these medals are not dished out with the rations. They are given to people only after careful consultation by a qualified committee considering the recipient's contributions to the developments of Canada.
I must say now that I have always had a slight prejudice so far as generals were concerned. This has been the result of my war experience. I remember particularly on one occasion my platoon was ordered to stay in the front line covering a wide front while the rest of the battalion retired to better positions because the Germans were going to bombard our front line trenches all to pieces. Our scouts indicated that they were bringing heavy batteries into position. I said, "Where does this order come from?" They said, "From General so and so". I shall never forget just prior to an attack in a snow storm on the Somme the carriers came up from brigade headquarters at six o'clock in the morning with great big tins of cold soup instead of rum. I said, "Whose order was this?" They said, "General so and so". I have always had a little bit of prejudice against generals but I must say that my experience of 15 years in this House of Commons have modified my views because of the service I realize that certain former generals have rendered to the Canadian people in the international joint commission, in the Canadian pension commission and in the Department of Public Works.
I know the deputy minister has a remarkable war record in the first and second world wars. However, one of his great achievements was when he was commander of

Supply-Public Works
Operation War Brides in charge of bringing back to Canada 66,000 war brides within a year. I know he has earned the personal gratitude of all kinds of war brides in Canada. Some time I will tell the deputy minister about a letter I received from a Cockney war bride who wanted me to tell him what a great deal he had done for her. However, regardless of having a minister and a highly qualified deputy minister, the department cannot run unless it has qualified staff and employees. I think we are extremely fortunate in that respect in the Department of Public Works having regard to senior officials, district officials and the permanent and the casual employees, and I shall have a word or two to say about casual employees in a minute or two.
I wish to say I speak with a certain measure of knowledge when it comes to the Department of Public Works. I have been in contact with officials of the Department of Public Works in Canada for 50 years, as an employee for four and a half hours over 51 years ago under Captain Armstrong who was the famous captain who sailed the Duchess on the upper Columbia in the latter part of the last century and the early part of this century, who was famous for his part in the operations of the Inland Waterways Transport Company in Mesopotamia in the first world war. I have written many letters to the department. I have read them all at headquarters since. First as secretary of a board of trade, then as secretary of a Liberal association, although I should not mention it, and then as secretary of a farmers institute.
I have also assisted the department on occasion by request in order to earn a few dollars when we were getting ten cents a box net for our fruit, as wharf inspector when someone was taken ill or as a timber inspector. I was an M.L.A. for four years and have been 15 years in this House of Commons. I therefore judge that I have laid a good foundation to indicate that I have some knowledge of the workings of the Department of Public Works, particularly so far as my own constituency is concerned. I might say that I know when every wharf was built, and who built it. I know the depth of every channel and of every lake and river. I know all the points of river bank erosion. I know all the areas in which there are snags where widening is required, and where dredging is required. I know the difficulties created by ice and silting from the upper reaches of the Columbia river and so on. Not only have I lived in the district for a good many years, I have made a point of studying the river
fMr. Herridge.]
system of the Columbia and the Kootenay because this subject has been of great interest to me.
I trust that I have established by now my right to speak with some knowledge as to the requirements of the constituency of Kootenay West. The other day I heard the minister's report to the house and I have read the departmental report with interest. I refer to the last one that was issued. I must say that the departmental report in recent years has improved. It is brief but it is clear and gives one a good general picture of the activities of the department.
As far as the minister's report to the house is concerned, I have just a few comments to make before I go on to making a few suggestions with respect to policies. I consider the administration of the department is excellent. One could not say that a few years ago. But one has only to be in touch with the department to realize what is being done today and to understand that any criticism we wish to make is not aimed at the deputy minister or at the senior officials but is aimed at the policy of the minister and the government.
I think the value of the property management division has been established in recent years. When that division was established I thought it was a good move. It is well evidenced by the efficient operation of the various public buildings throughout the country. I also think that the economics division was a necessary division to establish. It is required more than ever because of changing circumstances. For many years our population and our industrial development was somewhat static. Now we get unexpected development. I know that the department must find some difficulty with rapid development unexpectedly in one direction or another; an industry is established or the population increases on one side of a town instead of on another, and so on. Therefore the economic division of the department is more necessary than ever in order to make certain that the expenditure is required having in view all the information that can be obtained with respect to present requirements and future developments.
I was interested when the minister said that the department had expended 90 per cent of the money that was voted last year in the estimates, if I heard him correctly. While the hon. member who preceded me was extremely critical of that fact, we must remember that there was a period in 1952 and 1953 when the department expended only slightly over 70 per cent of the money that was voted. That was at the time when the whole departmental machine was almost bogged down. Since 1954 that situation has been steadily remedied. However, speaking for

this group and in view of the unemployment situation last winter, I could not understand why the department did not spend 100 per cent. I should like the minister when he replies to explain that question. There may be good reasons. Sometimes it is not possible to buy a site as expected or it is hard to obtain materials or there are property rights that have to be expropriated and sometimes there are legal reasons. But in view of the unemployment situation during the last year I should like the minister to explain more in detail when he replies why only 90 per cent of the money voted was expended in the last year.
I must say that the policy with respect to constructing small standard buildings such as post offices and R.C.M.P. headquarters in small communities has received the endorsa-tion, I think, of all parties and all members in the House of Commons. We have had several in my constituency in the last year or two. These small buildings are appreciated by the people in these small communities. They do something for the community. They set a certain standard. Only recently I read in the local paper in my constituency that an R.C.M.P. building has just been completed and the post office building has just been completed by the department in Nakusp. The person who writes the articles is quite capable of expressing opinions with some knowledge. This editor mentions how many people have suggested that the design of the buildings themselves is in keeping with the geography and the location and is an asset to the community and so on. I find that to be so generally with the small buildings. I shall have something to say later on with respect to the larger buildings. We hope the department will continue that policy of building these small, permanent excellent structures in the small communities of our country for post office purposes, for R.C.M.P. headquarters and other purposes.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that he intends to use more and more Canadian architects at home and abroad. We in this party support that proposal. We are pleased to hear about it. I might also mention that we hope the department also employs local architects wherever they are available and are competent to do the work undertaken in small cities and in small communities when buildings are being considered. There have been some cases in recent years where architects in Vancouver or some larger centre have been asked to design new buildings when there were local architects capable and qualified to do the work, as evidenced by plans they had already prepared for local hospitals, schools, and so on.

A word now about the employees of the department. We hope the department is pushing the civil service commission a bit in order to obtain the increase to which its employees are entitled. 1 want to suggest that in recent years the department has lost some excellent employees because of the scale of salary or wages that is being paid. Some of the men who now have to be replaced in my district had a very valuable background of experience. They understood pile driving; they understood dredging; they were good boatmen; they were good with tugs; these were hard working, experienced and capable young men who have been lured away from the department by the large companies connected with the logging and timber industry on account of the higher wages paid. I was talking to a young man last fall and he told me how much he preferred to stay with the department. He was in charge of pile driving and wharf construction. He was offered a much larger salary by a lumber company to take charge of its pile driving and booming grounds together with any dredging that might be required. So I urge that the department give consideration to this question of salaries or wages and make sure that these capable men are not lost to the public service, for it takes years for a man of that type to gain experience.
And now a word with respect to architecture and public buildings. I have here a cutting from the Montreal Star of March 12. It is an article written by Mr. Alan Jarvis. I do not want anyone to think that I wholly support Mr. Jarvis' conception of art. There is much with which I do not agree in what he wrote about large public buildings in Canada. However, there is one point which I think deserves consideration. Here is the suggestion:
My suggestion that the only solution to the problem of the ugliness of so many government buildings is to make slipcovers-made at the art gallery of Vancouver in the course of a public lecture- which has been widely reported, was neither a flippant remark aimed at "getting a laugh", nor the bilious fulmination of a professional curmudgeon. It was a simple cri-de-cceur made by an ordinarily sensitive citizen, and it is shared by a great many other Canadians, as the cheering response from the Vancouver audience, 800 strong proved.
I think Mr. Jarvis has a point and his point is that if the design of the larger buildings constructed in Canada were open to public competition, with a qualified committee to decide which designs should finally be accepted, such a procedure would offer an incentive to Canadian architects and an opportunity for a diversity of ideas in connection with these larger public buildings erected by the department in Canada. I do

Supply-Public Works
not like the large, square uninteresting glass structures without character that one sees nowadays, but I do suggest we could combine the functional, the beautiful and the permanent in a suitable manner. I am not one who goes to extremes on this question. I do know that the traditional architecture is insufficient to meet the requirements of today but surely there can be a blend of ideas which could produce a satisfactory type of public building in Canada.
So in this respect I support Mr. Jarvis' plea to the Department of Public Works to hold open competitions among the architects of Canada in connection with large public buildings which the department proposes to build. Public buildings are, of course, related to their sites just as houses are. Certain sites, or certain environmental situations suit certain types of public buildings. As long as the basic requirements of functionalism beauty are met, I think it is very desirable to add some diversity to our landscape.
Now I want to say a word about Operation Lemon Juice. This newspaper item reads:
Satisfied with the scrubbing job on D'Arcy McGee and the fair maiden they call Mollie-
I am quoting now from an article in the Globe and Mail by Walter Gray-
-senior officials of the Department of Public Works have given permission to clean up the remaining eight bronze statues on parliament hill.
I do not know where this idea comes from. I know that lemon juice and lime juice are good for certain conditions suffered by the troops, but I did not know statues suffered from these disabilities. I have made a point of looking at D'Arcy McGee's statue since it was cleaned, and to my mind it is just a shabby looking green mess. I do not know much about this subject, but I do know that very many people think it is entirely unnecessary to remove the patina from statues. It is interesting to note that when the statue of the former prime minister, Sir Robert Borden, was made, a patina was created artificially to give this statue an appearance similar to those which had acquired a patina as a result of age.
I should like the minister to inform the committee how much this treatment, this insistence on cleaning off the patina, is going to cost. Personally I will take some convincing that it has been worth while, or is necessary. I would much prefer to see the money spent on restoring and renovating what is known as lovers' lane. I have walked around the back of the building-
Oh.

Mind you, I have only been there because I wanted to see the beauty and do some botanizing. I would suggest there
[Mx. Herridge.]
is such a wonderful opportunity for landscaping right from the Rideau canal round to the supreme court building and that something should be done to give the public an opportunity to enjoy this fine scene and walk overlooking the river. As it is, this wonderful river walk is denied to members of the House of Commons and of the Senate, as well as to residents of Ottawa and visitors to the city. I would urge the minister to give instructions for the repair and renovation of what is known as lovers' walk, behind the parliament buildings.
Why?

So that its natural beauty and advantages may be enjoyed by all.
Now I want to say a word about my constituency. I suggest to the minister and to his deputy in all seriousness that they would be well advised to pay a visit to the Kootenays and see for themselves the developments that are taking place in the forest, mining and smelting industries. I think their presence is necessary in order that they may satisfy themselves about the correctness of the representations I make on behalf of my constituents and the justice of my representations. I suggest that they meet the departmental launch at Arrowhead, go down the Arrow lakes, the Columbia river and the river in the narrows and go as far as Castlegar; then go on by road along the Columbia river to the international boundary; then on to Nelson and take the departmental launch around Kootenay lake and travel back to Revelstoke via Trout lake or return to Nelson and visit the constituency of the hon. member for Kootenay East. I suggest that the minister and his deputy give consideration to my suggestion. If they come I will arrange a number of dinners by local organizations on a strictly non-partisan basis giving them an opportunity to meet the local people and learn their requirements.
If the minister and his deputy visit they should bring Captain Allen, chief of floating equipment for British Columbia. No one knows more about the problems of wharf location and the deepening of rivers than Capt. Allen because of his long experience as a dredge captain and his experience in wharf construction, riprap and so on. Experience sometimes means more than engineering degrees in terms of knowing local conditions concerning high waters, currents, et cetera. Local experienced people can anticipate future problems because of their knowledge and experience throughout the years.
I wish to express appreciation on behalf of my constituents for the building of the Galena bay wharf. Some were hesitant about

this but the building of the wharf has proved to be the proper thing to do. The road is under construction and soon hundreds of cars will be using it daily.
It was planned to spend $4,000 to tear down the Burton wharf but as a result of representations the money was spent to repair it. I just received word that ten boats from the United States have tied up at the wharf recently. This job was well done.
Conditions are changing. The channels must be deeper and straighter as booms are sometimes half a mile long. These new circumstances will have to be considered when plans are made for dredging from now on.
I suggest that when it comes to building new wharves and dredging, in addition to engineers the local residents should be consulted especially those who have been captains on tugs or have worked in the forest industry at booming. They know local conditions and can judge currents, and so on. Things are not always as they appear to be with respect to high and low water and much can be gained by consulting local people with experience. The Arrowhead wharf for instance was built in the wrong place. I was down here and did not know anything about it. It should be about a half mile further east. Navigation is affected by ice floes in the spring. Large chunks of ice six and eight feet high drift in around the wharf causing difficulty to the ferries and tugs. The channel also suffers from silting from the river.
Tourist traffic is increasing. There is a constantly increasing flow of water traffic from the United States and the eastern provinces. We are pleased with the launchways that have been built. The people of Slocan City, would like a launchway. Much work of this nature could be done in this district. These launchways are cheaper than standard wharves. If built soundly and if the piling is deep enough they are suitable for all the traffic on the lakes including pleasure craft, and small tugs. Having in mind that vessels larger than pleasure craft will tie up it may be necessary to put the piling down an extra five feet-I am not certain-I believe in time these launchways will replace many of the standard wharves as they require rebuilding and so on. I urge the minister and his deputy to give consideration to constructing launch-ways at Slocan, Riondel and Kootenay bay.
Of course everything cannot be done at once but these requests could be put on the departmental program and undertaken as money is available. The work should be done at a time when it will create the greatest amount of employment. Only people living within a radius of 15 miles of these works

I thank the committee. When I get on the Arrow lakes time means nothing. They need a new breakwater at Nakusp. The wharf at Nakusp is on a 10 per cent grade which makes it unsuitable for the typing up of small craft. A wing dam is also required at Arrowhead. A much wider and deeper channel is required in the river from Arrowhead south for some miles, because-I mentioned this last year-these tugs have to make a right-angle turn and they are pulling very long booms of the type used by the pulp and paper companies, which require much more room and greater depth. Therefore, a wider, deeper and straighter channel is required.
People are very pleased with the completion of the R.C.M.P. building in Nelson. The local authorities there tell me that it is a credit to the city of Nelson. It is attractive, is on an excellent site and is an addition to the city's architecture.
The people of Rossland also appreciate the fact that on further investigation the department has decided not to repair or renovate the old post office at Rossland but to rebuild it. I am quite sure the department was somewhat surprised when it was known what would be required to renovate and repair the old building. I am sure that, working in close co-operation with the city council the officials will be able to find a suitable site and erect a satisfactory building.
In concluding I do urge further consideration of the question of ventilation and air conditioning of the buildings at Nelson and Trail. The ventilation still is not satisfactory in the federal building at Nelson, particularly in the post office where they handle the mail and the lint comes off the bags. Trail should have air conditioning; it is much warmer there and conditions are quite uncomfortable for the employees at times. In fact, in the first instance I should have urged that air conditioning should be put into the larger buildings of the department where climate requires it.

I come to the end of my remarks. Some years ago there was some mention that the department was going to do away with the district office in Nelson. I can assure the department that the industrial development and the work that will be required of the department certainly necessitates the maintenance of a district office in Nelson. Someone has to be on the job to look after growing departmental responsibilities on the Kootenay, Arrow and other interior lakes and communities. That is all I have to say at this time. I thank the committee for being so generous to me on this occasion.

Mr. Chairman, I simply have a constructive suggestion to make to the minister. I would be very happy if all federal buildings which have been erected in the past or will be erected in the future, by his department could if possible, bear bilingual inscriptions to designate them. At the end of speeches made on the first item, I would like the minister to give me his views on the subject.

Mr. Chairman, the non-statutory estimates of the Department of Public Works for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961, amount to about $153 million, over $85 million of which are to be used on capital expenditures.
During the last fiscal year, the department's capital expenditures totalled about $110 million. Most of those capital expenditures cover works carried out under contract and for which the department had to invite public tenders. Of course, in all cases, the contract is supposed to have been awarded to the lowest tenderer, or at least, that is the system of award we believe the department should have used in the circumstances. The balance of its capital expenditures covers works carried out under contract, without public tender, by the hour or by the day, by teams under the supervision of departmental officials.
In a constituency located in the hinterland, such as the constituency of Villeneuve, which I have the honour to represent, except when construction of public buildings is concerned, the works carried out by the federal Department of Public Works, are fairly numerous, but their total cost is generally not very high. The cost of those works ranges from $2,000 to $5,000 and seldom exceeds $10,000. For that reason, each of those projects is carried

out by teams of men paid by the hour or by the day, under the immediate supervision of the department, as I explained a moment ago.
And so, those works carried out by the Department of Public Works in the constituency of Villeneuve, or in other similar constituencies, consist mostly in construction and reconstruction of docks and landing wharves on lakes and rivers, or again in dredging or clearing up rivers, or other similar works.
Furthermore, most of the time those works are carried out or completed at the request of municipalities, chambers of commerce or other public bodies which are usually familiar with the needs of their respective areas. Those works provide employment for a great number of workers and day labourers and when they are carried out as they should be, under the supervision of conscientious foremen, they cost very little and are very useful to the people of the areas concerned.
In the fiscal years 1949-1950 to 1956-1957 inclusive, in the constituency of Villeneuve, the federal Department of Public Works has carried out or has had carried out works of that type-and I do not include here public buildings-construction and reconstruction of wharves, deepening of rivers, to the amount of about $160,000.
From June 1957 until now, similar works have been done in the constituency, and I have no doubt that, in most cases, they were necessary, that most of them were carried out at the request of responsible organizations, and, I presume, under the supervision of conscientious foremen and under the immediate supervision of engineers of the Department of Public Works.
However, I have serious reason to believe that in Villeneuve riding, over the last three years, some works carried out on instructions from the department were performed in somewhat exceptional circumstances. I shall deal first with two cases in particular.
The first has to do with the reconstruction, during 1959, of a wharf located on the west bank of the Malartic river, range 4, in the township of the same name. The minister is well aware of this matter, since he ordered the case investigated. The investigation is perhaps not over yet, so I do not intend to go into details. However, for the information of the minister, I must add that as soon as I was informed that some irregularities had

apparently taken place during the reconstruction of the wharf on the Malartic river, I put on the order paper the following motion for papers:
For a copy of all payrolls showing the names of those employed, the period of employment and the amount paid to each person, in connection with the reconstruction, during 1959, of a wharf located on the west bank of the Malartic river, range 4, in the township of Malartic, Quebec.
The house knows what reply was given to that motion. As reported on page 2857 of Hansard, the Minister of Public Works answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are conducting an investigation at the present time, and I would appreciate it very much if the motion could stand until their report is received.
I then complied with the request of the Minister of Public Works.
A little later, at the request of the hon. Minister of Public Works and following his statement that I would be informed immediately the R.C.M.P. investigation was completed, I agreed to withdraw the motion temporarily.
Mr. Chairman, I later learned that at the very moment when I was notified that certain irregularities had apparently been committed in the reconstruction of the Malartic river dock, someone else had notified the departmental authorities.
This explains why, even before my notice of motion for the production of documents appeared on the order paper, orders had been issued for an investigation by the R.C.M.P.
I therefore have reason to believe that, should the investigation reveal that serious irregularities were committed, the department will take appropriate action under the circumstances.
That is all I had to say about this matter, Mr. Chairman, except that I have two questions to ask the minister.
My first question is divided in four parts: Who asked for reconstruction work at the Malartic river wharf? Through whom was that request transmitted to the department? Had a departmental inspector made an inquiry before the work began? What were his recommendations?
Mr. Chairman, that question is very im-not serve any practical purpose. The wharf has been of no use for several years, and cannot serve any practical purpose. The wharf was built in 1934 when there was no access
Supply-Public Works
road to allow for the development and operation of mines in Fourniere township, which is now within the limits of the city of Malartic, a few miles south of Malartic river, where the wharf was built.
A few years later, that is in 1938, the provincial government completed the road linking Amos with Malartic, and since then the Malartic river wharf, built in 1934, has been of no use to anyone nor has it served any purpose.
My second question, Mr. Chairman, is divided in two parts: what is the name of the man who acted as foreman on that reconstruction job and by whom was he recommended? What are the names of the suppliers of the material used on that job and who recommended them?
I trust the minister will be good enough to answer those questions.
And now, Mr. Chairman, I have another similar problem, or perhaps could we call it another similar scandal, on which I should like to draw the minister's attention.
This time it is a matter of river cleaning operations in the townships of Hebecourt, Montbray, Duprat and Duparquet, at the northwestern tip of the Villeneuve constituency. The rivers involved are the Kana-suta, the Mouilleuse, the Magusi and the D'Alembert, which flow into lake Duparquet.
Those river clearing operations were allegedly carried out in July, August, September and October 1959, that is to say from July 29 to October 10, 1959, judging from the dates mentioned on the payrolls which were produced following a motion for the production of documents dated May 23, 1960.
According to those payrolls, the foreman in charge was Rene Leroux, of Duparquet, province of Quebec, and it seems that the assistant foreman was his brother, Wilfrid Leroux, of the same place.
Again according to the same payrolls, the brothers Leroux were responsible for 16 labourers who were employed for periods of various durations.
Six day labourers are supposed to have worked throughout the whole project, that is from July 29 to October 10. They are Messrs. Ubald Sauve, Levesque, Nich Filipchuk, Omer Gregoire, Normand Tremblay and Alfred Lagrange.
Mr. Phillip Smith is said to have worked from July 29 until September 26. Messrs. Nich

Supply-Public Works
Peacosh, Albert Cameron and Marc Lagrange are reported to have worked from July 29 to August 15.
Mr. Patrick Dewar is supposed to have worked from July 29 to September 12. Messrs. Florian Dewar and Horace Lefebvre are reported to have worked from August 17 to October 10.
Messrs. Rejean, Simon and Jules Cloutier are supposed to have worked from September 14 to October 10, while Mr. Delphis Perron, is said to have worked from September 28 to October 10.
Total wages paid by the department to the persons I have just mentioned, including the Leroux brothers, amounted to exactly $6,896.60.
It should be noted, Mr. Chairman, that on every payroll, there is a typewritten note to the effect that all pay cheques are to be sent to Mr. Rene Leroux, Duparquet, P.Q.
On May 6, 1960, I received the following letter from Mr. Rosaire Lecavallier, of Duparquet, P.Q.:
Mr. Armand Dumas, M.P.
Dear Sir,
Allow me to ask you to provide me with a copy of the payrolls for the work done on the rivers flowing into lake Duparquet in 1959. In my view, there were some real scandals in this matter, as the pay cheques were made out in favour of persons who were unable to do any work. However, they were not cashed by those persons, but rather by government supporters.
That is why I should like to have the information above requested.
Yours sincerely,
Rosaire Lecavallier P.O. Box 87 Duparquet, P.Q.
In reply to that letter, I asked Mr. Lecavallier to supply me with further details.
On May 15, I received a letter from Omer Gregoire, of Duparquet, P.Q., one of the men whose names appeared in the payrolls I referred to a moment ago, in which he gave me additional information. I quote his letter, which was dated May 15, 1960:
Mr. Armand Dumas, M.P.,

Mr. Chairman, on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Public Works, I should like to offer a few general suggestions to the minister on the matter of town planning.
The construction of government buildings across the country can play a considerable part in the planning of urban centres where they are located, apart from the fact that their architecture and styling can also have considerable influence. (Text):
Many Canadian planning professionals and officials will have to deal in their own city and during their own careers with a total amount of urban building greater in extent, and more pregnant with import for human lives, than the whole of the London with which Sir Christopher Wren was confronted after the Great Fire.
(Translation):
And it is also in this respect that I would suggest to the Minister of Public Works to have his department resort as frequently as possible, I would even say whenever possible, to the services of professional town planners with regard to the location and construction of public buildings. As a matter of fact, there is no doubt that the erection of public buildings, if the site is integrated in the main plan of the city, is an important factor of renovation, and results, moreover, in higher real estate value which benefits the whole neighbourhood.
With regard to this matter, the Minister of Public Works will perhaps allow me to point out to him that, in view of the considerable development of the city of Montreal, federal services will, before long, be relocated in the Montreal district. It would be appropriate with regard to this matter, to consider immediately whether it would be opportune to connect this administrative development with the proposed C.B.C. development, the Jacques Cartier concert hall, now under construction and the existing town hall and court house, so that the eastern part of center town, might benefit from such a renovation of public buildings.
My other suggestion to the Minister of Public Works with regard to town planning is of a still more general character. It might be appropriate to consider carefully the great public projects proposed by the municipalities, so as to be able to determine whether the federal government might not, for reasons of national interest award some financial assistance with regard to some of those developments.
If this were done, Mr. Chairman, it would ensure the starting of projects of national

interest, which could be integrated in the functional development of the large cities and relieve the budget of those cities.
Until now, both parties limited their activity to specific projects without trying to integrate the interests of the various levels of government. It is not a matter of granting further subsidies, but rather of finding, among the municipal works being planned, sections which, by their nature, location or function, are of national interest and thus justify the intervention of the federal government.
As an example, I might mention the throughway which is planned by the city of Montreal along the river, something which might, to a large extent, be included in the cost of redeveloping the port of Montreal.
Such a procedure would seem to be the most practical and quickest way of providing employment in urban centres, and of helping municipalities that are unable to pay for such vitally important projects, while not going beyond works of truly national interest and without raising problems as to the prerogatives of the various levels of government.

I was glad to hear that the government intends to do something about removing restrictions affecting house building. The easing of restrictions is something that we in the opposition have been advocating for a long time, and we think they should have been removed long ago. They were responsible for imposing a definite hardship on people wanting to build new homes, to say nothing of the chaotic conditions in the house building industry created by tight money.
In Fort William house building permits for the first six months of the year are down to the lowest level in 10 years. If this low record in house building had been caused by a declining demand for new homes it would have to be accepted, but the house building contractors and individuals seeking loans claim it is not so. They claim there is a heavy demand for new homes and they have the facilities and the manpower to build them.
When Canada's chartered banks were forced out of the mortgage market because the interest rate climbed higher than 6 per cent, the limit the banks are allowed to charge, one of the most logical sources of money supply was cut off, leaving insurance companies to dominate the field of money lending. But these companies, for reasons which they have not disclosed, seem to have stopped lending money in Fort William and Port Arthur, except for a few token loans. I am told that these large insurance companies are allocating their mortgage money almost exclusively to cities such as Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Edmonton, Vancouver and a few other large centres. It is most unfair for these companies which take hundreds of thousands of dollars out of the lakehead area in premiums to confine their investments to other communities.
I wonder whether it would be possible to impose some regulation whereby insurance companies would be obliged to invest in the area a given percentage of what they collect in premiums in order to persuade them to desist or to compel the elimination of a flagrant policy of discrimination.
Mr. Chairman, on June 21 I drew the attention of the minister to a resolution passed by the city council of the corporation of the city of Fort William urging the federal government to give serious consideration to the construction of breakwater facilities for
Supply-Public Works
the protection of McKellar and Mission islands where large tracts of industrial property face lake Superior within the city of Fort William and I asked the minister to give an indication of the government's intention in the matter.
The minister replied that as and when any determination is made of the matter an announcement will be made. At the time there was no opportunity for me to enlarge on the question. I wish therefore to seize the occasion to point out the need of breakwaters fronting our major undeveloped industrial area and I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to say a word about the reason why we are asking the government to give this matter serious consideration.
For the benefit of those who may not know, the city of Fort William is located at the outlet of the triple-mouthed Kaministikwia river which empties into lake Superior. It is the largest city in northwestern Ontario. The city of Port Arthur, incidentally, is catching up fast and is only a few hundred behind in terms of population. Fort William has always been recognized as a rendezvous or meeting place as far back as 1655 and there is no doubt in the minds of the people living in the lake-head area that with the seaway terminal now under construction it will not be very long before the facilities will have to be expanded considerably to take care of the steady increase in deep-sea waterways traffic.
A number of European shipping lines have established office facilities at Fort William with a view to operating a regular service between the lakehead and continental Europe. It is obvious, therefore, that every effort should be made to develop harbour facilities and to provide protection for the natural harbour layout that is part of Fort William.
The two islands which form part of the harbour frontage of the city of Fort William are exposed to lake Superior and require protection. It has been recommended before that a breakwater be constructed paralleling the two islands and running south from the present breakwater which protects a portion of the mainland fronting on Port Arthur. With the potential industrial development that may come with the availability of natural gas and the seaway the lakehead is taking an upward swing and it is imperative that the project should receive favourable consideration in the 1961 estimates.
At the present time, the Canadian Pacific railway owns a large area of land on McKellar island which could be put to industrial use and there is considerable property on Mission island which can hardly be developed without breakwater protection. For clarification, I should say that these two islands are separated by deep navigable water.
