At the present time ocean-going ships are docking at Fort William but are only able to take a portion of their normal load and this is due entirely to the present depth of the Kaministikwia river. Dredging the whole of this river and the outlets through McKellar river and Mission river is also required if full use is to be made of the natural harbour facilities available in this area.
Another obstacle which is retarding the full use of these two islands and which must be removed is that at the present time there is only one bridge connecting the mainland with Mission island, and a second bridge connecting Mission island with McKellar island. In the event that anything happens to the bridge connecting the mainland it will have the effect of separating both islands completely from the mainland. It will be seen, therefore, that another bridge between the mainland and Mission island is absolutely essential. The building of another bridge would also remove the deterrent against the immediate developing of the two islands for potential industrial expansion, including the possibility of a steel mill, which possibility is very real, since the Premium Ore Company, headed by Cyrus Eaton, the chairman of the board of the Steep Rock Iron mines, has an option on Mission island for such a project.
I realize that the construction of a bridge in this particular area is not entirely a federal government responsibility. I am of the opinion that the cost would be shared with the province of Ontario. However, we must bear in mind that the bridge would also serve as a highway for further development of harbour facilities. It is generally conceded that when expansion in the seaway dock now under construction becomes necessary the only desirable area available will be on the islands fronting lake Superior.
Another matter of considerable importance with which the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Labour are particularly familiar is the need for a new public building to house the old dilapidated national employment office. This building was the old post office which was vacated by the postal department nearly 30 years ago. It is a relic of the gay 90's, a fire-trap, and totally inadequate for the service which it is rendering today. It is used by thousands of unemployed daily, especially at the peak of unemployment in the spring of the year.
Last year the Department of National Defence closed the armoury at Fort William because it was condemned by the fire marshal. This building was an old hockey arena converted into an armoury at the beginning of world war II. The building was demolished and the site which has a frontage

of 140 feet on Archibald street and 273 feet on Leith street is now vacant. It is located in the central part of the city and is readily accessible to all commercial areas. It has been transferred to the Department of Public Works and the expectation has been that a building would be erected by the federal government on this site during 1960.
It is no secret that the Department of Labour has made such a recommendation and it was understood that a new building was on the Department of Public Works program for commencement early in 1960 and that plans for details and space requirements were under way. I presume that the minister in an effort to cut the estimates to the bone, to enable the Minister of Finance to come up with a surplus, considered the building at Fort William one of the first casualties.
During the discussion of the trans-Canada highway resolution on March 30 last I pointed out the poor condition of the highway west from Fort William to the Manitoba boundary which, with the exception of a few stretches, is now no better than it was four months ago. This condition prevails also on the highway east of Port Arthur for practically 200 miles. Just recently the Ontario minister of highways, Mr. Cass, visited the lakehead area and I wish to quote from an editorial in the News-Chronicle of Port Arthur, a newspaper which is not at all unfriendly to the government of Premier Frost, which indicates that a very sad state of affairs exists in so far as the trans-Canada highway is concerned. I quote:
Highways Minister Fred Cass has come and gone. He visited the lakehead, travelled the trans-Canada highway between here and Schreiber, then flew back to Toronto. He came, he saw, he condoned.
It seems Mr. Cass, like his fellow minister in the department of planning and development, W. M. Nickle, believes the best defence is offence. So when he met with a group of citizens in Port Arthur complaining about the delay in completing the road connecting this area with eastern and western area he gave them the "you never had it so good treatment".
He admitted that the Frost government might have been dilatory for 14 years, but during his two years as highways minister the situation had improved remarkably. His department was spending more money in northwestern Ontario than the area deserved.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: Order. It seems to me the hon. member is discussing a matter which comes under the provincial government of Ontario. If he can relate it to the estimates that we are now considering I will agree that he is in order; otherwise, it seems to me he is discussing a provincial matter.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
On a point of order, I am speaking about the trans-Canada highway, toward the construction of which the federal

treasury pays 50 per cent. I am merely reading an editorial which describes the condition of the highway in which the federal government is very much concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: It seems to me that the upkeep of the trans-Canada highway is the responsibility of the provinces although the federal government does pay part of the construction cost. I understand the hon. member to be discussing the upkeep of the trans-Canada highway which, unless I am wrong, is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. If the hon. member can point out his authority for saying it is the responsibility of the Minister of Public Works and the department I will agree with him.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: The authority I point out is a very simple one. The federal government pays 50 per cent of the cost. If the government is paying 50 per cent of the cost of any project, then I assume it has a responsibility for it. I am therefore pointing out what has already been described, namely the condition of the highway.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
I do not think the hon.
member can assume from the fact that the Department of Public Works pays 50 per cent of the construction cost that the minister has any responsibility for the upkeep.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
I point out the fact that this particular highway has been about 20 years in the building. Some people have been working on it here, there and everywhere for 20 years. The federal government has paid or is paying 50 per cent of the cost. Therefore, I say, I have the right to speak about the trans-Canada highway and the responsibility of the federal government. I think it is true that the provincial government assumes the responsibility of the actual construction, but if the federal government is paying 50 per cent of the cost then I would say it certainly has a responsibility to tell the provinces when and how it should be done.
The editorial is very clear in its judgment of the trans-Canada highway, both east and west of the lakehead area. We are not dealing with secondary provincial highways which are the responsibility, it is true, of the provincial governments; we are talking about the trans-Canada highway financed by this federal government. For that reason I think I have the right to speak loud and clear about the condition of this stretch of the trans-Canada highway.
May I say something about the unseemly attitude of a provincial minister in saying that the highway is all right, in the face of the condition it is in. It is almost unbelievable. I should like to ask the minister to get
Supply-Public Works
in touch with Premier Frost and secure from him the promise that the renovation of the trans-Canada highway west of Cochrane and up to the Manitoba boundary should have priority over any other provincial highway in the eastern part of the province.
I say that the provincial government is spending proportionately far more in the eastern part of the province than in western Ontario. I point out that the lakehead is the natural gateway to the prairie provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. We share a common interest. We are the key to their communication system in which the movement of goods from eastern Canada is an important factor in the life of northwestern Ontario.
I urge the minister to make sure that this apparent neglect of the trans-Canada highway through the northwestern part of Ontario is not allowed to continue. An assurance of this fact will be appreciated by the people of the area.
In conclusion, I ask the minister to give consideration to these important projects, not just the usual consideration, but rather serious thought, as being beneficial not only to Fort William but to the lakehead, northwestern Ontario and the nation, when one considers the whole picture, just as much as the St. Lawrence seaway is of benefit not only to the communities along the seaway but to the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Laurier, the question of the hon. member for Villeneuve on the order paper was entered as an order for return on June 6, 1960, and tabled by the Secretary of State on June 10, 1960. The information which we supplied did not disclose any irregularities, but it appears that Duparquet is in the same riding of Villeneuve and in the same area as Malartic. It also appears that we laid the whole matter before the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, as the hon. member for Villeneuve was good enough to say, some time before it came to his attention. It has been in the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for several months now. It appears that Malartic is only part of it, according to the hon. member for Villeneuve, and that the instances are more widespread and include Duparquet lake.
In the circumstances, therefore, as the matter is already being investigated with regard to Malartic and as it would appear that this other incident involves the same kind of circumstances and occurred under the same auspices in the same district, the government would be greatly obliged to the hon. member for Villeneuve if he would submit to us any affidavits and information

Supply-Public Works
he has so that the investigation already under way in the district of Malartic can be widened to include Duparquet lake. Would the hon. member be good enough to do this so that we can get to the bottom of this matter? If there is any wrong-doing we want to prosecute to the full extent of the law.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had copies of these affidavits prepared today for the minister and I will be very pleased to send them to him. However, I should like to emphasize the point to the minister that although these contracts were carried out in the same constituency they did not come under the same order and were far apart in location. One job is in the centre of the constituency a few miles north of Malartic and the other job is at least 75 miles from Malartic. The two jobs are absolutely different. They do not come under the same item in the department.
I am sure of that and I am also sure that when the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were instructed to conduct an inquiry into the case at Malartic they were not instructed to conduct an investigation with regard to the works carried out in the Duparquet region. If the minister can tell me that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have already been instructed to conduct an investigation in the Duparquet district I will be very pleased to hear it. I am sure they will do their job and I am also sure that the department will do everything in its power to prosecute those who have committed irregularities if there have been irregularities.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: Then the hon. member agrees to supply us with this information. So that the matter can be gone into immediately by the police, would the hon. member be good enough to tell us why, when he had the information as long ago as May 23, he has withheld this information about alleged fraud until tonight when he seems to have known all about the matter.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: That is where the minister is wrong. It was not for me to run to the minister's office the minute I receive a letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: There is your question on the order paper on May 23.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have the floor. On May 23 when I put my question on the order paper I did so to satisfy myself first that work had been done in the township of Duparquet. 1 did not know these people who had written me and just because they had written and asked for an investigation I was not called upon to jump and run to the minister's office and ask him to conduct an investigation immediately. In fact,

if I had done that the minister would have said that he could not do so without having something on which to base an investigation. I could not go to the minister and sign an affidavit that irregularities had been committed with respect to the work in the township of Duparquet. I got all the information I could and as soon as I had it I brought it to the attention of the minister. I got the information last Friday, July 15.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Villeneuve object to us putting this matter in the hands of the police tomorrow morning?

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: That is not his responsibility; that is yours.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: That is the responsibility of the Department of Public Works. After I have given the affidavits to the minister the minister can instruct the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to investigate if he has not already done so.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: There are many lakes in the hon. member's tremendous riding of Villeneuve. Would he be good enough to tell me whether he has any further information, in addition to the Malartic and Duparquet cases, that will assist the mounted police? He seems to be aware of a great deal of fraud going on in his riding. Can he help me as to any other lakes?

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: I have told the committee that I am aware of two cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: Is that all you know?

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: I know of two cases so far, but I wish the minister would have an investigation conducted by his own department or by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police with respect to all jobs carried out during the last three years in my constituency. I am not saying that irregularities have occurred on all these jobs but we can suspect that there may be some irregularities. We do not know. Particularly if any of these works were recommended by the same people and especially if the foremen were recommended by the same party the minister might find it proper to conduct investigations into all the jobs performed in the constituency of Villeneuve.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: I too should like to ask the minister to have an investigation conducted in order to clear up a matter. In the year 1956 a protection wall was built on the Richelieu river at the village of St. Charles.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: What year was that?

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
In the year 1956 before we came to power. A man hired his son 12 years of age and also his brother-in-law and paid

them tor work which they never did to the extent of $877.80. I should like to ask the minister who the contractor was, who recommended him and also who recommended that the work be done. That was in the year 1956 under the previous administration.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question before he takes his seat?

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: Would he tell us when this information first came to his notice and if he has ever brought it to the attention of the Department of Public Works?

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: The reason why I have not given any names is that the case is before the courts now. You can have the information if you want to read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: I am just learning about this matter for the first time even though it happened as long ago as 1956. My information is that the matter is under investigation and I believe it is an the hands of the Department of Justice. I will correct myself if I find that information is not correct.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext: And therefore not subject to discussion in the house.

maintopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC DISTRICT OF ABITIBI.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will not speak about protection walls and work being done on the Ottawa river in my county because we do not have any. However, I should like to point out one thing. In my recollection for over 40 years all the different ministers of public works have always followed the practice in dealing with contracts of awarding them to the lowest tenderer. This was true also of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs when he was in charge of the Department of Public Works. There have been a very few exceptions when the contractor was financially unsound or when he had worked for the department previously and did not give complete satisfaction to the department. I should like to say that I have something new from the present Minister of Public Works. I do not need any affidavits. I have all the letters over here to prove that the present Minister of Public Works is doing away with that precious custom of giving contracts to the lowest tenderer.
On March 23, 1960 and on March 30, 1960 tenders were opened for two post offices, one at Hudson Heights in the province of Quebec and the other at Hudson. For the first one there were four tenderers who were as follows: Stuart & Stuart, Montreal, $23,825; Gray & Gareau, Hudson, province of Quebec, $21,650; S. R. Wilson, Hudson Heights, $19,950; Arthur Langlois, Ste Rose de Lima, in
Supply-Public Works
the county of Hull federally but the county of Papineau provincially, $16,750. In that case, the contract was awarded, not to the lowest tenderer but to the second lowest, S. R. Wilson, Hudson Heights, at a cost of $19,950, being $3,200 more than the lowest tenderer.
In the second case there were seven tenderers for the post office at Hudson. The first tenderer was K & M Construction, Montreal, $35,450; Sinclair Supply, Ontario, $28,396; Do-rion Construction Ltd., $27,990; Alain Enterprises Inc., Dorval, $25,990; Gray & Gareau, Hudson, province of Quebec, $25,890; S. R. Wilson, the same one from Hudson Heights, $24,868; Arthur Langlois, Ste Rose de Lima, in the county of Hull federally but the county of Papineau provincially, $21,783. In this instance the contract was awarded again to S. R. Wilson, Hudson Heights, for $24,868, a difference of $3,085 between his contract and the tender of Mr. Langlois.
Then Mr. Langlois decided to write to the present minister and I am quoting from a photostatic copy of what he wrote. This is in French:
(Translation):
Dear sir,
In the last month, your department has invited tenders for the building of the two above-mentioned post offices and on two occasions I was the lowest tenderer. Since then, I have not yet been instructed to start the job, except for being asked for additional information about my past record (since I am a new contractor for the department) and about the tender application forms.
Thinking that some other information was missing, I had my son phone Mr. Gardner last week end to inquire about this, but he replied that everything was all right and that only the final decision remained to be given, but he did not know exactly when that would be.
As for me, I do not understand this delay. It seems to me that, after giving proof of my experience, my efficiency and financial soundness, I should start the work immediately.
Therefore, I appeal to you because you are well acquainted with all those projects and I would be grateful for some explanation in this regard.
Respectfully yours,

On May 17, the minister himself wrote the following to Mr. Langlois:
I thank you for your letter of April 22, 1960 in which you inquire about the awarding of contract for those two projects.
In order to make a complete assessment of your tenders, we have conducted a thorough investigation concerning the works you performed, and their quality, and into your general experience and financial situation. We have visited the Mont Joli area where you carried out many of your works before moving to Ste Rose de Lima in 1959.
The inquiry revealed that, though your financial means were considered adequate, the over all construction of your buildings, we were told, was

Supply-Public Works
of very low quality. It has been noted that the finish of your work was of a very inferior grade. Apparently, a houseowner had to supervise your work to get better results and, even in spite of that supervision, there were some defects.
In view' of this situation, I cannot but recommend to the treasury board to by-pass your tender and to allocate the contract, in each case, to the second lowest bidder.
(Text):
On receiving that letter, the contractor, Mr. Langlois, wrote back to the minister and I quote from a photostatic copy of what he wrote at the time:
(Translation):
Sir,
I just read your letter of May 17, 1960, and I was most surprised when informed of your decision with regard to the above-mentioned post offices. I am given as a reason that my previous work was carried out in a rather inferior manner and I am apparently not qualified to work for your department. I do not know, sir, who gave you such information-if anybody did-which caused your decision; but I may tell you that it is quite inaccurate and false. Some scandalmongers may be at the root of that story. I challenge anyone to ask any of my customers whether they were satisfied with my work; for, in the past, they were always the ones to recommend me for new contracts.
However, Mr. Minister, could it not rather be a purely political motive, in view of the fact that following an interview with Mr. Bourbonnais, M.P. for Vaudreuil-Soulanges, on Thursday, May 19 at 3.15 P.M., the latter advised me after a lengthy conversation that he had promised those jobs to contractors in his constituency and that if he backed out "they would kill him" in the next elections. Those were his very words. At that point, I said I did not blame him and that I understood his position. Furthermore, Mr. Bourbonnais promised me his support for other future contracts.
Mr. Minister, I am not blaming the people responsible for present developments, but I do not want my reputation tarnished without cause. Every job I have done in the past was found quite satisfactory. I did jobs ten times more difficult than post offices, and I was always respected just as I respected my contracts.
(Text):
In my opinion, this is a very poor explanation given by the minister for refusing to grant the contract to the lowest tenderer. He says that he had certain inquiries made around Mont Joli to see if this man, who had never worked before for the Public Works Department, was giving satisfaction to those for whom he had worked. I do not know where the minister got his information, but I state now that he was ill-informed. Then the minister passed on this information to the treasury board, when it really amounted only to hearsay that he had obtained from the region of Mont Joli. I can prove that what the minister said about the inefficiency of the contractor is completely untrue. I have

here a letter from the C.N.R. The division engineer first sent a telegram which was in these words:
Arthur Langlois,
253 St. Joseph Blvd.,
Hull, Quebec.
This is to state that you have performed services for the Canadian National Railways in providing an extension to our express building at Mont Joli in 1956, value of contract being in the vicinity of $16,000 and that your work was very satisfactory.
M. B. Martin Division Engineer, C.N.R.
In the letter which is not quite the same, the writer says this:
To whom it may concern:
This is to certify that Mr. Arthur Langlois constructed an extension to our Express Building at Mont Joli, Quebec, in 1956, valued at approximately $16,000.
This contract was successfully completed in a workmanlike manner to the complete satisfaction of the railway.
Yours truly,
R. M. Wickwire, Building Engineer.
(Translation):
In addition, Mr. Langlois did some work for the Banque Canadienne Nationale, a well known corporation which is not in the habit of squandering its money or letting it go down the drain. Here is the letter he received in that regard on July 11, 1960.
To whom it may concern:
This is to certify that Mr. Arthur Langlois, general contractor, of Mont Joli, was responsible in the year 1956 for carrying out an enlargement and improvement work on the Banque Canadienne Nationale building at Mont Joli, P.Q., under contract from the bank.
The work consisted of building a new vault and carrying out considerable improvements to the building, both outside and inside, at a cost of approximately $35,000. It was done in a satisfactory way.
(Text):
This is the reason why I am questioning these reports the minister has said he received from Mont Joli relating to the past construction of Mr. Langlois. I prefer to take the view-and I am positive that this is the reason-that the minister is returning to an old principle which was abandoned over 40 years ago and is going back to the patronage system in order to please some members of parliament, as was stated by the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges. I really think that the minister, by doing so, is not doing justice to the federal government which did away with this kind of patronage system in years past.
In the government of Ontario, for things much less important than that, three ministers were obliged to resign their seats because they bought shares in a natural gas

corporation which was not a property of the government. Here we have a man who has the responsibility of granting contracts, as has been done over the last 40 years, to the lowest tenderer if the lowest tenderer is financially sound and can execute the work to the satisfaction of the department. I have here proof that Mr. Langlois has been working for Canadian National Railways and that he has been working for the Canadian Bank of Commerce to their perfect satisfaction. He was refused. I do not know where the minister obtained his information. However, if he intends to go back to the old patronage system, I believe there is only one thing for him to do, namely to resign his seat as a minister of the crown.
Furthermore, I believe the Prime Minister put him in his present post because he seemed to be so greatly scandalized over what happened with respect to the printing bureau. He seemed to be posing as the most just man we could find on earth. If the Prime Minister had known that he would resort to that kind of practice in the Department of Public Works I am sure he would never have placed him there and I think the Prime Minister should ask for his resignation right away.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I should be delighted to supply the last speaker with the particulars of the Hudson post office and Hudson Heights post office. Two of our investigators unanimously found this in connection with the Hudson post office, and I am reading from the report. Extensive investigation into the qualifications of the lowest bidder, who was Arthur Langlois, has shown that while the financial resources of Mr. Langlois are adequate, he possesses a very poor record of workmanship. I also note that he was the same person who was the low bidder on the Hudson Heights post office and that for the same reason he was not granted the contract. As a matter of fact, in an order for return on July 15 to the hon. member for Levis' question No. 64, all this information was given by me to the house. In addition to Hudson and Hudson Heights there are three other instances: Ga-liano, British Columbia; Eskasoni, and also Whycocomagh in Nova Scotia. There will be another one which I hope the hon. member for Levis will raise, namely St. Maxime de Scott. I want him to raise that in due course. I do not blame him for not doing so until the items come up for consideration.
As the hon. member for Hull, who made that astounding peroration knows too well, it is our duty to see to it that the public interests are protected and that one of the grossly irregular things for any department to do would be to grant a contract to a
Supply-Public Works
person who was incompetent to execute it. That was clearly demonstrated by the manner in which the printing bureau and the printing bureau building was erected. That was brought out fully to the satisfaction of everyone.
Since the hon. member for Hull asked the question and suggests that during the prior administration no contracts were awarded except to the lowest tenderer, I might also say that I should be happy to produce for him, since he has asked for them, a list of the contracts not awarded to the lowest tenderer during the years 1955 and 1956. If he wants me to do so I should also be glad to follow that up and give him the contracts, and the time and place, for just as many years back as he would care to go, if he would just name to me now the years that he would like me to investigate. Perhaps he would like the information back to the beginning of the 22 years of Liberal administration. That information is available.
I am not suggesting at this time that in many of those instances there were not good and justifiable reasons for not awarding the contract to the lowest tenderer, particularly since a new deputy was appointed in 1954, namely General Young. If the hon. member for Hull will let me know what he wants we will go back as far as he likes. If he wishes us to do so we will also produce the reasons why the lowest tenderer did not get the contract. In this sense it must be obvious to all members of the committee that the Department of Public Works is doing a very much needed public duty by keeping scallywags and incompetent people, even though they might be friends of the hon. member for Hull, from getting contracts which they might be incapable of fulfilling.

The minister says that he has found in years past some contracts which were not given to the lowest bidder. There is no doubt about that. As I said, that might be the case on some occasions when a contractor was financially unsound or when he had previously worked for the department and his work had not been found satisfactory. These are the reasons which have been followed in the past. But the minister tells us he had an inquiry made by an official of his department. I do not know where he went or if he went to see the Conservative candidates over there to try to find fault. But there is one thing I have here. I have a telegram and a letter from the C.N.R. which is a responsible firm. Whenever they give a contract they supervise to see that it is carried out properly. I have a letter here from another important firm,

Supply-Public Works
the Banque Canadienne Nationale, and when they give a contract they supervise it even more closely than any government does. They answer that they are completely satisfied with the contractor who worked for them.
If the minister wants to give us names, I hope he will give us all the names. I hope he will tell us who gave information about Mr. Langlois. If that information is wrong, I want Mr. Langlois to have the right to sue these people for defamation. Let the minister give the names of the informants. Let the minister say where this information was obtained, and give us the names and addresses of these informers and then I think Mr. Langlois will be in a better position to prove that the information the minister was given is really not the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: How many years back would you like me to go for this information?
Give the information you are asked about your own administration.

I want to have this information first of all, and then, if he likes, the minister can go back as far as he pleases, but let him give us all the information, not information chosen to suit his own purposes.
(Translation) :

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all, I want to thank the Minister of Public Works, most sincerely for the attention he always gave to any request of the chambers of commerce and the economic committees in my riding.
I also want to thank his deputy minister and all his staff for the kind information they always gave me each time I resorted to their services.
Of all requests made by the various public bodies in my riding, there are two very important ones I want to point out to this house tonight, because they are both of capital importance to the economic development of my district.
There is, first and foremost, Mr. Chairman, the improvement of Chandler harbour, which has been asked for the last few years. You are doubtlessly aware that this town has a very prosperous industry, the Gaspesia Sulphite, which manufactures pulp. That company recently decided to build another factory for newsprint which will give employment to a number of people, not only in Chandler, but in the adjoining parishes. I therefore hope that the Department of Public Works will follow up this request, because

it is of great importance, more particularly so that my riding in the future may benefit from a new industry.
The chamber of commerce also requested the improvement of the harbour in Grande Riviere. There again, another company is waiting for this project to be accepted or carried out by the department, before starting to construct a factory for processing fish.
Mr. Chairman, like all citizens in my riding, I would like my district to benefit from those two industries which are absolutely essential, as I said before, for the development of Gaspesia.
I have no doubt whatever that this request will be agreed to, since the departmental officials have already begun to consider the matter. In fact, a sort of small scale model has been prepared. Surveys were made and all the stone required was found on the spot. I trust those works and experiences will continue and that, in the near future, I shall be able to tell the people of my constituency, that those long-awaited improvements will be carried out.
Mr. Chairman, a moment ago, I heard the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) express deep concern for the fact that two contracts, according to him, had not been granted to the lowest bidder.
Allow me, first of all, to tell you that since I have been elected member for the constituency of Gaspe, I have never bothered recommending one contractor instead of another. The only thing I want to have for my constituency are achievements on the part of the Department of Public Works, and as long as I obtain those achievements, I will not bother with the name of the contractor or of the builder.
However, Mr. Chairman, as you know, the cost of living has gone up very much and I find it very strange that contractors can accept contracts to build post offices for $16,000, when the estimate cost of such a building is around $22,000 or $25,000. I feel that what happened in my constituency is now happening again. I have not looked into the matter, but I must say that I have received several complaints about a contract for the building of a post office having been granted to someone outside the constituency. In fact, while that post office was being built to help solve the unemployment situation, the contractor came in my constituency with two or three employees and a sub-contractor so that the building of that post office does not provide any work for the people of that community.

Mr. Chairman, the other day the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), upon learning that a building was to be constructed in his constituency, urged the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to call tenders in his constituency only and not outside. May I say that I share his views, regardless of what the hon. member for Hull may think about it.
Thus, Mr. Chairman, I ask the Minister of Public Works that from now on tenders for the construction of small post offices be called in my constituency only and it matters little who gets the contract, whether he be a Liberal, a C.C.F.'er or a Conservative, I am sure that jobs will thus be provided for our people at home and that it will help reduce unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, I also heard the hon. member for Hull refer to two bids and call for the resignation of the Minister of Public Works. I wonder why the hon. member for Hull, when he was sitting in this house and his government was in power, did not call for the resignation of the person who let the contract for the national printing bureau, which was to be built for a certain amount and eventually cost three times that amount? I regret that at that time, the hon. member did not raise cries of scandal and-
Was anything proven in that matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I feel it would have been much more reasonable for the hon. member, at the time, to report the fact to the house, because it involved a building running into millions of dollars, whereas now, he attaches vital importance to the construction of post office buildings costing $16,000 or $18,000.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the Minister of Public Works has always made it a point to let contracts in a fair and equitable manner.
I also know that in my constituency, a contractor got a contract to build a house on Anticosti island. He was to do the work early in the season; unfortunately, there was some delay, and instead of having his materials delivered by ship, the contractor had to use aircraft. At the time, I asked that he be allowed some compensation; however, I was told it was against government policy. I made no complaint, Mr. Chairman; I accepted that decision though I knew full well that extras had been allowed in such cases as the national printing bureau.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I think if you went back over the years, we would find a number
Supply-Public Works
of things. I would be very pleased if the Minister of Public Works could supply us with information on all contracts awarded over the past 12 or 15 years.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English) referred to me in connection with the printing bureau. He told me that I should have asked the minister to resign when the contract was granted for the construction of the printing bureau. So, it seems that the hon. member for Gaspe got his information only at the public accounts inquiry where the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), acting as a prosecutor, judge and everything else, could not find one irregularity, because the contract had been granted to the lowest bidder. Besides, those who suggested that this building was built in a swamp did not know a thing about it. This building was built on a gravel soil; in fact, we had to dig 17 feet lower than expected because of the large stones and the enormous rock deposits which were there. So, if there was water in the basement, it is not because it was built in a swamp. If the Minister of Public Works, who led the famous investigation, had known something about construction, he would have known that, by being forced to dig 17 feet lower than expected, they went at least 20 feet lower than Brewery's creek level, which caused water to seep through rock. But, all the nonsense we heard at this inquiry was false and came from the fertile imagination of the present Minister of Public Works who did not know a thing about it and who acted as a judge, and especially as a man that was shocked by works that had been properly prepared and properly carried out, after tenders that had been called in a regular manner.
When additional works were performed on instructions from the same Minister of Public Works, those works were carried out at the same price per cubic foot.
At all events, I know for one thing that I have no knowledge at all of the riding of the hon. member for Gaspe, but since he knows nothing of the Hull riding, he should at least stop talking about it.

Mr. Chairman, may I put a
question to the hon. member for Hull?
Could the hon. member for Hull explain why it is that, after completion of the printing bureau, an amount of $850,000 had to be spent to repair the air conditioning system, which was a scandal in itself?

Supply-Public Works

The architect gave a clear enough answer to this question. And when a fine architect like Mr. Cormier who is known throughout the world answers such questions, his word has a lot more weight than that o f the member who has just spoken, and of the minister who does not know anything.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to add only a few words to what the member for Hull has just said.
At the outset of my remarks, I extended hearty congratulations to all employees of the Department of Public Works, and among them were people in the department's employment for many years. Some of those conscientious officials made certain statements at the time that building was under construction; the hon. member for Hull must know that subsequently attempts were made to get rid of them.
(Text):

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to prolong this discussion but I should like to draw the attention of the minister to a statement he made a while ago and ask him if he would not consider revising it because I think it is a serious one and it is that which has led to all this discussion. I believe the minister made this statement as an aside because there was no reason for his saying it. He was discussing another matter altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: What year was that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just a moment ago.
Approximately 15 minutes ago.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. What the minister said- and he will correct me if I have written it down incorrectly-was this. He indicated that all those who built the printing bureau were incompetent and inefficient. I am now inviting the minister to give consideration to an amendment of that statement. I say to him that it is an unfortunate statement and an inaccurate statement. I do not think the minister would want to do an injustice to those contractors and particularly the main contractor of the building, namely Concrete Construction Limited.
I shall go a step further than inviting the minister to amend his statement. I doubt very much if the minister who has had a great deal of experience in the courts as he

told us the other evening would make this statement outside the house.
Having said that I should like to put on the record the opinion of the United States equivalent to the Canadian Queen's printer who came here no longer ago than last year and inspected the printing bureau. His statement appears in an article in the Ottawa Citizen of November 5,	1959, entitled
"Printing Bureau Wonderful Job". The article states:
The United States public printer describes the printing bureau in Hull as "one of the finest printing plants I've ever seen. I only wish we had had the architect for some of our plants."
Raymond Blattenberger, who In Washington corresponds to the Queen's printer in Ottawa, made a special trip here to look over the controversial Hull plant which was subject to a parliamentary committee inquiry last year.
He was Charmed
The public printer described himself as charmed by the plant's design, surprised at the efficiency of its operation.
Ernest Cormier, Montreal architect responsible for the building, had a rough ride from Conservative members of the committee which inquired into the plant's building.
"He certainly did a wonderful job as the architect," says Mr. Blattenberger.
The public printer's plants in Washington are multiple storey affairs. "The best operation is always on one floor and that is what you have here," he said.
Informed that there had been considerable criticism of the design of the plant, Mr. Blattenberger said that was to be expected.
"No matter how good a job you do you can always be investigated and criticized," he said. "Whoever the architect was for your plant, he did a magnificent job."
In the light of the statement of a perfect stranger who came here and visited the building which is certainly a treat to the eye, and in the light of what the minister said, I ask him in all seriousness if he will not in fairness give consideration to revising the statement he made.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to add to what I have said by saying that this term "incompetent and inefficient" includes all those who were responsible for the planning and the execution of this building and particularly the architect, Mr. Cormier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would invite the minister to listen the name-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: My hon. friend knows all that very well. He was at the inquiry. He heard all about it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: He would not dare to.
He certainly would not.

To come back to the case mentioned by the hon. member for Hull, can the minister tell us who made the inquiry into the technical ability of Mr. Langlois, and who signed the report that the minister received?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: As the hon. member for Levis knows, because he himself was a very competent parliamentary assistant to the minister of public works, two officials of the department made the investigation. As my friend well knows, since he often took this position, we do not disclose the names of those officials because if we did we could not expect them to act in a straightforward and fearless manner.

Will the minister give the names of those who were interviewed, because this is an important accusation against a man who never worked before for the Department of Public Works. I should like to have the names of the informers who said that his work was not satisfactory. That is what I want to get. If the minister does not want to give the names of those who made the inquiry that is all right, but I should like to have the names of those who spoke about the contract; otherwise, I would ask the minister to change the information he gave to the treasury board because he was ill informed and he ill informed the treasury board which is certainly a very grave thing to do. I accuse him of playing party politics in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I always consider the source; that does not beget any reply.

This is a very important question. Here is a case where tenders were submitted and the lowest one was $6,080 lower than the others. I think the committee should know because this is an important amount and I do not think the architects or the employees of the department who made the report will object to the minister giving their names in the committee. We have to know whether it is only a letter that the minister received from someone or whether it was really a report from a man who had some experience in the business and made a thorough inquiry to find out exactly whether Mr. Langlois was really qualified or not.
This comes to my mind because the hon. member for Hull has given two responsible firms. The minister will agree with me that the Canadian National Railways is quite a responsible company and the Banque Cana-dienne Nationale is also a reliable institution.
Supply-Public Works
In all fairness to a man who has lost a contract I would ask the minister to give the committee the information as to who made the report, who investigated this man, and also give the committee the contents of the report; otherwise we shall have to take other means through the public accounts committee to find out exactly what happened. We shall have to ask the two employees of the department to appear before the committee and state exactly how they found out and on what grounds they made the report which they gave to the minister that Mr. Langlois had not the technical ability to carry out the contract.
(Translation):

The Liberals are the ones who made the report.
(Text):

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: In reply to my friend, they were senior officials.

That is quite all right, Mr. Chairman. I think we are entitled to know. This is a very serious case and the minister must realize it. Here we are putting aside a contractor who did work for two big institutions. He had letters of commendation saying that the work he did was satisfactory to them. Surely if he can work to the satisfaction of the Banque Canadienne Nationale and of the C.N.R. he is capable of doing work for the government of Canada. The minister should tell us who are the employees in the department who made the report, where the investigation took place, where did they meet Mr. Langlois and all the information necessary in the circumstances.

The consideration that the minister is showing for the two officials of his department will be very touching to all those who remember the way he dragged the names of officials through the mire only two years ago in a committee of this house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Did the officers of whom the minister speaks consult the Canadian National Railways officials and the Banque Canadienne Nationale to ascertain from them whether the work of this contractor was satisfactory? Will the minister answer my question?
He is not even listening.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall item 327 carry?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I ask the hon. member-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, sir. My question is this. When I put my question to the minister he was talking to the Minister of Labour and was not even listening. Now, surely, we on this side of the house are entitled to a little more respect

Business of the House
than that from a minister of the crown. The simple question which I asked, to which he paid absolutely no attention, was whether those investigators of the Department of Public Works consulted the officers of the Canadian National Railways and of the Banque Canadienne Nationale to ascertain whether or not work done by the low tenderer was satisfactory?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no idea whom they consulted but I do know that they reviewed three projects which this contractor had carried out and came to the conclusion they did without any influence from anyone. I can only count on their report and on their good judgment because, according to the deputy minister, we have always found them to be competent and fair and always strictly honest and impartial in making their judgments.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire what the business is for tomorrow and I think on Friday the house leader gave some indication that he would tell us what we would do on Wednesday. Perhaps he could extend that for a greater portion of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, as I announced last week, we shall take the estimates of the Department of Finance. If concluded, we shall continue with the estimates of the Department of Public Works. On Wednesday we shall continue with the estimates of the Department of Public Works followed by the estimates of Department of Veterans Affairs. I do not think I can go
farther than that; it depends on the progress of the house as to how we manage with regard to the other estimates. I should like this week, if we can, to complete the estimates of the privy council, the Secretary of State and legislation, which are not large departments, but we shall have to see just how we shall make out on Tuesday and Wednesday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the house leader. I make an appeal to him in this case. It is that tomorrow, as the house leader knows, there is to be a dedication ceremony at Laurier House at 2.30 p.m. Since this dedication ceremony, attendance at which is at the invitation of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, is one which affects those of us who sit on this side of the house in an especial manner because of the fact that Laurier House was the residence of two former Liberal prime ministers of this country, I ask the minister if he will not have the house adjourn for a period of one hour from two to three o'clock to enable those of us who sit on this side of the house to attend the dedication ceremony. Otherwise it will not be possible for us to give the kind of consideration to the estimates of the Department of Finance that those estimates require. The request is not an extraordinary one and under the circumstances I wonder whether the minister would not consider it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The request will be considered and a report will be made tomorrow on orders of the day.

It being four minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.
